README.md.overview: Top-level README that introduces both the Virodh AI gateway (the product) and the Threat Guard inspection engine underneath it. It gives the one-line commands for running the stack, the high-level ingress-to-policy pipeline diagram, the layer-by-layer table of detectors, and the repository layout separating project code from the upstream OmniSafeBench-MM toolbox. It is the first document in the guided tour and sets up the stage names (ingress, extract, detect, fuse, policy) the later steps follow.

sections.title: Virodh product and commands
sections.explanation: Defines **Virodh AI** as an OpenAI-compatible reverse proxy: clients keep their SDK and only change the `base_url` to `/v1`. The PowerShell block lists the main entry points: the combined launcher script, the engine-only server, key management, the end-to-end SDK test, and the Docker Compose scale-out command. These commands map directly onto later tour steps (gateway entry point, evaluation, deployment).

sections.title: Threat Guard engine pitch
sections.explanation: Describes the engine's core idea: read an image the way an attacker hopes only the model will (faint, mirrored, QR-encoded or encoded text) and return an **ALLOW / REVIEW / BLOCK** decision with evidence before the request reaches the model. It also credits the OmniSafeBench-MM toolbox the project builds on.

sections.title: Quick start setup
sections.explanation: Setup instructions for the research API: provider keys are set as user environment variables (never in files), a Python 3.11 venv is created with `uv`, and the app is run with uvicorn. Note that the test suite is designed to run offline because the hosted classifiers are mocked, which matters for CI and reproducibility.

sections.title: Pipeline diagram and layers
sections.explanation: The ASCII diagram is the mental model for the whole codebase: INGRESS validates and re-encodes, EXTRACT recovers hidden text, DETECT runs four detectors, FUSE produces one risk score, POLICY gates the request, and allowed requests later pass through the output guard. The table ties each layer to its purpose and the research idea that inspired it (for example cross-modal composite detection and a trust-separating envelope). The closing line notes which classifiers are hosted and that everything else runs on CPU.

sections.title: Adversarial image engine
sections.explanation: Summarises the separate engine for pixel-level adversarial perturbations: statistical, frequency, prediction-consistency and local-region detectors plus a learned model. A key design constraint is stated explicitly: on its own it can raise ALLOW to REVIEW but never BLOCK. The paragraph also links to documented caveats, keeping performance claims honest.

sections.title: Repository layout
sections.explanation: Separates project-owned code (`guard/`, `virodh/`, `tg_plugins/`, `app/`, `eval/`) from the unmodified upstream toolbox directories. Noting that `guard/` has no upstream imports explains why the engine can be reused by the gateway without pulling in benchmark code.

sections.title: Reproducing the evaluation
sections.explanation: The ordered script sequence for the benchmark: sample the dataset, build splits and benign hard negatives, generate test cases, scan them with the guard, calibrate thresholds on the **validation** split only, generate responses, and compute metrics. Keeping calibration off the test split is the methodological point to notice.

docs/VIRODH_GATEWAY.md.overview: Design document for the Virodh gateway. It explains the React/Node dashboard in front of the engine, the per-request pipeline inside each stateless worker, the public API and error codes, per-key policy fields, low-level security decisions, scaling measurements and limitations. It is the most detailed map of the `virodh/` package and is referenced by the tour's overview step, with sections that line up with later steps on the API, policies, testing and deployment.

sections.title: Purpose and entry points
sections.explanation: States the goal: one approved path between many applications and any AI model, with central policies and an audit trail. The table lists the URLs the single process serves (website, console, developer guide, OpenAPI docs, legacy research lab).

sections.title: React and Node dashboard
sections.explanation: Describes the human-facing layer: a Node/Express server on port 3000 that owns user accounts, sessions, roles and CSRF checks, serves the React build, and passes `/v1` straight through to the Python engine. Separating human accounts (Node) from API-key auth (engine) means the dashboard never reimplements inspection.

sections.title: Worker architecture
sections.explanation: The numbered pipeline inside each stateless worker: streamed body cap, hashed API-key lookup, shared rate limit, parsing into inspection units, guarded inspection with bounded slots and cache, policy, forwarding with a circuit breaker, output guard, response headers, and the request log. The module table maps each step to a file in `virodh/`. It notes that no new libraries were added beyond FastAPI, uvicorn, httpx, pydantic and the standard library.

sections.title: Public API and errors
sections.explanation: Documents `POST /v1/chat/completions`, the extra `virodh` metadata object and `X-Virodh-*` headers, how blocked requests look (HTTP 200 refusal with `content_filter`, or HTTP 400 error), and why streaming is buffered until the reply is checked. It also covers the inspect-only `/v1/guard/scan` endpoint and the full catalogue of OpenAI-style error codes grouped by status.

sections.title: Per-key policies
sections.explanation: Lists the policy fields (`mode`, `review_action`, `block_response`, `output_guard`, `envelope`, `adversarial`, `blocked_phrases`, `denied_topics`, `allowed_models`) and their effects. The explanation of operator rules is the key design idea: whether a request is acceptable depends on the service, so the exam-integrity rule is opt-in and should be validated in monitor mode first.

sections.title: Low-level design decisions
sections.explanation: A compact security rationale table: streaming body limits, overlapping text chunks, forwarding the inspected bytes to avoid TOCTOU, SSRF restrictions, concurrency slots released only when the worker thread ends, load shedding, single-flight and caching (never caching fail-safe verdicts), fail-closed behaviour, circuit breakers, shared SQLite state, hashed keys, CSRF-safe console headers, CSP and privacy defaults.

sections.title: Scaling and load results
sections.explanation: Explains how to run multiple workers and replicas, a Windows-specific finding (shared listening socket stalls under `uvicorn --workers`) and the fix of independent gateways behind a least-connections balancer. The load-test table and the bullet list explain why gateway overhead scales with processes while image inspection is CPU-bound, and that overload produces fast 503s rather than uninspected forwarding.

sections.title: Testing summary
sections.explanation: Summarises the test layers: offline unit and integration tests with a fake guard and mock provider, an end-to-end run with the official OpenAI SDK, a regression check for the Windows stall, load tests and headless UI checks. The coverage paragraph enumerates the gateway behaviours exercised, from auth and refusals to SSRF targets and key revocation.

sections.title: Known limitations
sections.explanation: Candid limits: inherited detection limits, dependence on hosted classifiers (with fail-safe holding when all are down), buffered streaming, SQLite suitable for a single host only, uninspected audio/files/tool calls, and a single admin role in the legacy console.

docs/threat_model.md.overview: Short threat model that defines what Threat Guard protects, who the adversary is, which attack goals are in scope, and which are explicitly out of scope. It frames the rest of the codebase: detectors, inspection resolution and the output guard all follow from the assumptions stated here. It is part of the tour's opening overview step.

sections.title: System under protection
sections.explanation: Describes the deployment: an application receives image plus text from an untrusted party and forwards it to a vision-language model, possibly after pre-processing such as QR scanning. Placing the guard in front of the whole application means it sees exactly what the user submitted.

sections.title: Assets and adversary
sections.explanation: The assets are the model's instruction hierarchy, the application's decisions and people affected by generated content. The adversary controls the image (and often the prompt) and knows common multimodal jailbreak families, but cannot change the guard's configuration or classifiers, which is the trust boundary the design relies on.

sections.title: Attack goals and measurement
sections.explanation: Two goals are in scope: **hijack** (instructions hidden in an image) measured exactly by checking whether the reply contains a harmless canary marker, and **jailbreak** (harmful requests carried by images) measured with an LLM judge. Using a canary gives an objective success signal for injection tests.

sections.title: Key assumptions
sections.explanation: QR attacks matter mainly for applications that decode QR codes, since tested models cannot read them reliably. The guard inspects images at the same resolution the model receives, which closes the trick of hiding content through downscaling.

sections.title: Adversarial perturbations
sections.explanation: Pixel-level perturbations are only partly in scope: they are measured against a local surrogate classifier because hosted models expose no gradients. This is why the adversarial engine may raise ALLOW to REVIEW but never BLOCK on its own.

sections.title: Out of scope
sections.explanation: Lists what the first version does not cover, such as attacks optimised against the hosted model's own vision encoder, audio and video, multi-turn or multi-image splitting, non-English text and handwriting. Stating these makes the evaluation claims bounded and honest.

config/virodh.yaml.overview: Main configuration for the Virodh gateway: runtime limits, storage, admin access, upstream providers, the public model map and the policy profiles seeded on first start. It is loaded by `virodh/config.py`, which allows environment variables to override any `server` value. Provider keys are never stored here; each upstream only names the environment variable holding its key.

sections.title: Header and conventions
sections.explanation: Comments explain the gateway's role and two conventions: secrets stay in environment variables, and every `server:` field can be overridden with `VIRODH_<UPPERCASE_NAME>` for container deployments.

sections.title: Server limits
sections.explanation: Request-path limits: body and image size caps (the body cap allows for base64 overhead), images and inspection units per request, scan concurrency per worker, a bounded wait queue with a timeout for load shedding, the fail-closed scan timeout, upstream timeouts and pool size, the verdict cache, remote images (off by default), and circuit-breaker thresholds. These values are read throughout `gateway.py` and `openai_compat.py`.

sections.title: Storage and admin
sections.explanation: The SQLite database path, log retention and an opt-in prompt preview that the comment marks as local-demo only. The admin block names the environment variable for the console token, whether loopback clients may skip the token, and the playground rate limit; `security.py` enforces these rules.

sections.title: Upstream providers
sections.explanation: Each provider entry gives a base URL and the env var name of its key, plus an offline `mock` upstream used for load tests and demos without provider quota.

sections.title: Public model map
sections.explanation: Maps the public model ids clients send to an upstream and the provider's real model name, with a display label and token defaults. Some entries carry a `max_tokens_cap` or a larger default for reasoning models; `upstream_payload` applies these. `default_model` is used when a request omits `model`.

sections.title: Seeded policy profiles
sections.explanation: Four profiles are seeded into the database on first start and can then be edited in the console: `default` (enforce), `monitor` (shadow mode), `public-sector-strict` (API errors and enforced adversarial findings) and `exam-integrity`, which adds a plain-language denied topic checked by the policy classifier. This shows how operator rules are expressed as data rather than code.

tg_bootstrap.py.overview: Import-time bootstrap module that must be imported before any upstream OmniSafeBench-MM module. It loads secrets from `.env` (and on Windows from the user registry environment), then monkey-patches the upstream YAML config loader so `${VAR}` placeholders are expanded from the environment. This lets the guard, gateway and benchmark code share one setup without modifying upstream files, as described in the tour's gateway entry-point step.

sections.title: Module docstring
sections.explanation: Documents the two side effects and the reason for them: no edits to upstream files, and API keys live only in the environment, never in YAML.

sections.title: Path setup and constants
sections.explanation: Adds the project root to `sys.path` so both project and upstream packages import correctly. `_VAR` is the regex for `${NAME}` placeholders and `REQUIRED_ENV` lists the provider key variables to look up.

sections.title: Environment loading
sections.explanation: `_load_env` uses `python-dotenv` if available (without overriding existing values). On Windows it also reads missing variables from the `HKEY_CURRENT_USER/Environment` registry key, because values set with `setx` are not visible in an already-open terminal. Errors are swallowed so a missing key is reported later, where it is needed.

sections.title: Recursive placeholder expansion
sections.explanation: `_expand` walks strings, dicts and lists and substitutes each `${VAR}` from the environment. An unset variable raises a clear `RuntimeError` that points to `.env.example`, so misconfiguration fails loudly instead of sending empty credentials.

sections.title: Patching the upstream loader
sections.explanation: Wraps `ConfigLoader._load_yaml_file` so its result passes through `_expand`. The `_tg_patched` flag makes the patch idempotent if the module is imported more than once. Monkey-patching keeps the upstream toolbox unmodified.

sections.title: Import-time side effects
sections.explanation: Both functions run on import, which is why other modules import `tg_bootstrap` purely for its effects (often with a `noqa: F401` comment), as `virodh/server.py` does.

virodh/config.py.overview: Loads `config/virodh.yaml` and applies typed environment-variable overrides so containers can tune the gateway without editing files. It resolves the database path relative to the project root and caches the result for the process. Every gateway module reads its settings through this file, as described in the tour's entry-point step.

sections.title: Imports and config path
sections.explanation: `ROOT` is the project root. `config_path` lets the `VIRODH_CONFIG` environment variable point to an alternative YAML file, which is useful for tests and deployments.

sections.title: Typed casting
sections.explanation: `_cast` converts the raw environment string to the type of the existing YAML value. The `bool` check comes before `int` because in Python `bool` is a subclass of `int`; otherwise `true` would fail to parse as an integer.

sections.title: Cached load with overrides
sections.explanation: `load` parses the YAML with `safe_load`, then overrides every `server` key from `VIRODH_<KEY>` env vars. It also handles specific overrides for prompt preview, database location and the loopback admin exemption, and stores an absolute `db_path`. `lru_cache(maxsize=1)` makes it a per-process singleton.

sections.title: Accessors and reload
sections.explanation: `server()` is a shortcut for the server section. `reload()` clears the cache and reloads, which tests can use after changing environment variables.

virodh/server.py.overview: The FastAPI application that assembles the whole Virodh process: the public gateway router, the admin console API, the website and console pages, and the legacy Threat Guard research routes. It builds the shared `GatewayState` at startup, warms up models in the background, applies security headers and CSP, and normalises errors so `/v1` callers always get OpenAI-shaped bodies. It is the central file of the tour's gateway entry-point step.

sections.title: Imports and bootstrap
sections.explanation: The docstring lists development and multi-worker run commands. `tg_bootstrap` is imported for its side effects (environment secrets, upstream config patch) before other project modules. Constants point to the UI folder, the legacy dashboard and the legacy body-size limit.

sections.title: Gateway state construction
sections.explanation: `GatewayState` is a dataclass holding config, guard config, store, inspector and upstream clients, plus readiness and warm-up info. `build_state` opens the SQLite store, seeds policy profiles, prunes old logs, and accepts optional `transport` and `guard` arguments so tests can inject a fake HTTP transport and a fake engine.

sections.title: Exit with supervisor
sections.explanation: When a supervisor starts the worker, a daemon thread waits for the parent process to exit and then terminates the worker. On Windows it waits on a process handle via `ctypes` instead of reading stdin; the docstring explains that a blocking stdin read can hold a C runtime lock and stall other threads.

sections.title: Lifespan and warm-up
sections.explanation: The async lifespan optionally enables periodic stack dumps for diagnostics, then builds state unless a test has already injected one. Model warm-up runs in a background thread so the server accepts connections immediately while `/readyz` reports 503 until `ready` is set. On shutdown it closes only resources it created itself (`own`).

sections.title: App and security headers
sections.explanation: Creates the FastAPI app with its OpenAPI description and defines the fixed security headers and a strict Content Security Policy (`script-src 'self'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`). An optional `TG_API_TOKEN` protects the legacy research API.

sections.title: Edge middleware
sections.explanation: An HTTP middleware applies early size checks to the legacy and admin APIs based on `Content-Length`, checks the optional legacy bearer token, then adds security headers to every response. CSP is skipped for the docs pages, which need their own scripts, and each response is tagged with the worker PID for debugging load balancing.

sections.title: Error normalisation
sections.explanation: Exception handlers return OpenAI-format error bodies for `/v1/` paths and simple JSON elsewhere. Validation errors report the first invalid field. The catch-all handler logs details on the server only and tells the client the request was not forwarded, which supports the fail-closed design.

sections.title: Router mounting
sections.explanation: The gateway and admin routers are mounted with `include_router`, keeping each feature in its own module. Legacy research routes are mounted under `/api` inside a `try` block, so the gateway still starts if those modules fail to import; `LEGACY_OK` records the result. Static UI files are mounted under `/ui`.

sections.title: Page routes
sections.explanation: Simple routes serve the website, console and developer pages with `Cache-Control: no-cache`. `/lab` serves the legacy dashboard or redirects home if the legacy routes did not load.

virodh/gateway.py.overview: The public, OpenAI-compatible API of Virodh. It authenticates the API key, applies rate limits, parses the request into inspection units, runs inspection, applies the key's policy, forwards allowed requests upstream, checks the reply with the output guard, and records every outcome. `run_chat` is the core pipeline and never raises; every failure becomes an `Outcome` with an OpenAI-style error. This is the main file of the tour's step on how clients call the gateway.

sections.title: Imports and global state
sections.explanation: The docstring lists the endpoints and the accepted auth headers. `STATE` is a module-level slot that `server.py` fills at startup (and tests can pre-fill); `st()` raises if the gateway has not started.

sections.title: Outcome record and errors
sections.explanation: `Outcome` collects everything about one request (status, body, headers, inspection, action, reply, timings, usage, error) so responding and logging share one object. `oai_error` builds an OpenAI-format JSON error response.

sections.title: Size-capped JSON reading
sections.explanation: `read_json` rejects oversized bodies early from `Content-Length`, but also enforces the cap while streaming, because chunked uploads have no length header. It requires a JSON object and maps parse errors to `invalid_json`.

sections.title: Authentication and rate limit
sections.explanation: `authenticate` extracts the key, looks it up in the store, rejects missing or revoked keys, and loads the key's policy (falling back to `default`). If `count` is true it records a hit in the shared rate-limit window and returns 429 with `Retry-After` when the limit is exceeded. It returns either a tuple or a ready response, which callers distinguish with `isinstance`.

sections.title: Headers, metadata, reasons
sections.explanation: `_virodh_headers` and `_meta` expose the decision, risk, cache use, policy and latency both as headers and as a `virodh` object in the body. `_short_reason` gives end users only a category or rule name, never the text recovered from the image, so a block message does not echo hidden content.

sections.title: Pipeline: parse, inspect, block
sections.explanation: `run_chat` resolves the model, checks policy and key allow-lists, and parses messages (with an SSRF-guarded fetcher for remote images). Inspection errors map to specific fail-closed responses: overload gives 503 with `Retry-After`, timeout 504, ingress errors 400, anything else 503. If the policy is in enforce mode and the decision is BLOCK (or REVIEW with `review_action: block`), it returns either an API error or a refusal completion with `finish_reason: content_filter`.

sections.title: Forwarding and output guard
sections.explanation: Allowed requests are rebuilt with `upstream_payload` and sent upstream; an open circuit breaker or provider error becomes a clean 503 or passed-through status. When `output_guard` is on, each choice is checked with `check_reply` against every unit's report; in enforce mode a suspicious reply is replaced and marked `withheld`. Monitor mode forwards but records `monitor_forwarded`. `_fail` sets the error body and a default action of `rejected` or `error`.

sections.title: Request logging
sections.explanation: `log_row` builds the audit record: decision, action, risk, timings, token usage, and truncated SHA-256 hashes of the prompt and images rather than raw content. A prompt preview is stored only when the config allows it. `record` updates metrics and writes the row, logging but not failing on write errors.

sections.title: Chat and scan routes
sections.explanation: `chat_completions` authenticates, reads the body, runs the pipeline, records it, and returns JSON or an SSE stream re-emitted from the already-checked reply. `guard_scan` accepts either OpenAI messages or a simple `input` and `images` shape, inspects without forwarding, and returns the decision, `would_forward` under this policy, and per-unit evidence.

sections.title: Models, health, metrics
sections.explanation: `/v1/models` lists models allowed for this key and policy without counting against the rate limit. `/healthz` is liveness, `/readyz` returns 503 until warm-up finishes and then reports provider key availability, inspector stats and breaker state, and `/metrics` serves Prometheus text.

virodh/openai_compat.py.overview: Translates between the OpenAI Chat Completions wire format and the gateway's internal model. `parse_chat` turns a request into inspection units covering every text chunk and image the model would see, `upstream_payload` builds the exact request forwarded to the provider, and the response helpers produce OpenAI-shaped completions, SSE streams and errors so existing SDKs work unchanged. It supports the tour's step on how clients call the gateway.

sections.title: Constants and BadRequest
sections.explanation: Defines accepted roles, a strict regex for base64 image data URLs, and the security notice added to forwarded requests that contain images (the trust-separating envelope). `BadRequest` carries an OpenAI error code, parameter path and HTTP status, so validation failures map directly to API errors.

sections.title: Data records
sections.explanation: `ImageRef` remembers where each image sat in the request and its bytes, MIME type and hash. `Unit` is one inspection job: a text chunk optionally paired with an image from the same message. `ParsedChat` bundles units, images, the latest user text and full texts for phrase rules.

sections.title: Chunking and data URLs
sections.explanation: `_chunks` splits long text into overlapping windows so a phrase that crosses a boundary is still seen whole by one inspection. `decode_data_url` checks the length before decoding (approximating base64 overhead), decodes with `validate=True`, and rejects empty images.

sections.title: Parsing into inspection units
sections.explanation: `parse_chat` validates the body and walks every message, including system, assistant and tool turns, so forged history is inspected too. Remote URLs are fetched only when enabled, and unknown part types such as audio or files are rejected because they cannot be inspected. Each image becomes a unit with its message's first text chunk, and other chunks become text-only units. Identical units are deduplicated by hash, and image and unit counts are capped.

sections.title: Building the upstream payload
sections.explanation: Copies the client request but forces `stream: false` so the reply can be checked before release. Remote images are replaced with data URLs of the bytes that were inspected, which removes a time-of-check/time-of-use gap. When the envelope is enabled and images are present, the security notice is inserted as a system message. Default and capped token limits from the model map are applied.

sections.title: Response builders
sections.explanation: `error_body` builds the OpenAI error object, `completion` builds a complete chat completion (used for refusals), and `message_text` extracts text from string or list-of-parts content.

sections.title: SSE re-emission
sections.explanation: `sse_chunks` replays an already-checked completion as OpenAI-style server-sent events: a role delta, content in small pieces, any tool calls, and a final chunk with the finish reason. The `virodh` metadata rides on the last chunk as an extra field that SDKs ignore. An optional usage chunk and `[DONE]` close the stream, matching OpenAI behaviour.

virodh/security.py.overview: Low-level request security helpers for the gateway: extracting the client API key, deciding who may use the admin console, and fetching remote images with SSRF protections. They enforce the console and remote-image rules described in the gateway design document and are used by `gateway.py` and the admin router, as covered in the tour's step on how clients call the gateway.

sections.title: API key extraction
sections.explanation: `api_key_from` accepts a case-insensitive `Bearer` token in `Authorization`, or falls back to `X-API-Key` / `api-key` headers, so OpenAI and Azure-style clients both work. `LOOPBACK_HOSTS` lists the host names treated as local.

sections.title: Loopback detection
sections.explanation: `_is_loopback` requires both a loopback client IP and a loopback `Host` header. Checking the Host header blocks DNS-rebinding pages that resolve an attacker domain to 127.0.0.1. `_host_only` strips the port, handling bracketed IPv6 addresses.

sections.title: Admin access rules
sections.explanation: Every admin call must send `X-Virodh-Console: 1`; because browsers need a CORS preflight for custom headers cross-origin and the server never approves it, other sites cannot drive the console (CSRF protection). A configured admin token is compared with `hmac.compare_digest` to avoid timing leaks; otherwise only direct loopback clients are allowed if the config permits.

sections.title: SSRF-guarded image fetch
sections.explanation: `fetch_remote_image` accepts only plain http(s) URLs without credentials, resolves the host first and rejects any non-global or multicast address. It disables redirects, uses a short timeout, requires an `image/*` content type and caps the streamed size. The docstring notes the remaining DNS-rebinding window between resolve and connect, which is why remote images are off by default.

config/guard.yaml.overview: Configuration for the Threat Guard engine: ingress limits, extraction tuning, hosted classifier endpoints and fallback chain, detector switches and weights, adversarial-engine behaviour, local demo options and policy thresholds. The header states that weights and thresholds are starting values and that thresholds are calibrated on the validation split. `guard/engine.py` and its detectors read it through `load_guard_config`.

sections.title: Ingress limits
sections.explanation: Size, pixel and format limits for images, the maximum prompt length, and the model input side length. The comment says the latter must match the benchmark plugins so the guard inspects at the same resolution the model sees.

sections.title: Extraction tuning
sections.explanation: Thresholds for OCR confidence, when to retry with mirrored or rotated views, the ink-contrast level below which a line counts as near-invisible, and the conditions for running the faint-text boost pass only on document-like images.

sections.title: Hosted classifiers
sections.explanation: Defines the prompt-injection classifier and an ordered fallback chain of policy classifiers across providers; on rate limit or error the next one is used. Live use fails fast (leading to a fail-safe REVIEW), while batch evaluation overrides the rate-limit settings to wait, so quota errors do not distort results.

sections.title: Detector switches
sections.explanation: Enables the four detectors and sets fusion weights. `required: true` means that if the detector errors, the request cannot be ALLOWed, which is how fail-safe behaviour is configured. The obfuscation detector has a lower weight because it only amplifies other evidence.

sections.title: Adversarial engine
sections.explanation: Turns on the adversarial-image engine in scans and sets `can_block: false`, so it can raise ALLOW to REVIEW but never BLOCK on its own, because of natural false positives and the use of a local surrogate model.

sections.title: Local demo options
sections.explanation: Options for a local presentation only: comparing with an unguarded model (with truncated and blurred output), and saving live scans to a log. The comments say never to enable these on a public server, and a keyword list excludes sensitive categories from the comparison.

sections.title: Policy thresholds
sections.explanation: The profile (where `strict` can only lower thresholds), the REVIEW and BLOCK risk thresholds chosen from plateaus found by calibration on the validation split, and a floor that forces at least REVIEW when an instruction aimed at the AI is found inside an image.

guard/engine.py.overview: The `ThreatGuard` orchestrator, which runs one scan through the stages ingress, extraction, hosted classifiers, detectors, fusion and policy, and returns a `ScanReport` with timings and evidence. It is the central file of the tour's step on core schemas and orchestration: the gateway's inspector calls `scan` for each inspection unit, using thresholds from `config/guard.yaml`.

sections.title: Imports and detector list
sections.explanation: Imports each pipeline stage from its own module, so the engine only coordinates them. `DETECTORS` is a module-level list of detector instances that share the `Detector` interface, so the engine can run them without knowing their concrete types.

sections.title: Constructor and detector names
sections.explanation: The constructor loads config if none is given, optionally enables audit logging, and creates a thread pool for parallel classifier calls. `detector_names` returns only the detectors enabled in config.

sections.title: Ingress, extraction, items
sections.explanation: `scan` validates input (raising `IngressError` on bad input) and runs extraction, recording per-stage timings. It then builds the items to classify: the user prompt, untrusted segments recovered from the image (skipping the first segment and very short text), and a composite text combining prompt and image text for cross-modal checks. `item_ids` maps each item back to its segment.

sections.title: Parallel hosted classifiers
sections.explanation: The prompt is classified in a separate call from the image-derived items; the comment explains that a long framing in the prompt could otherwise sway verdicts on image text. Prompt-injection scores are requested for the prompt and each untrusted segment in parallel. Failures are recorded as `verdict_error` or `pg_error` instead of raising, so later stages can apply fail-safe rules.

sections.title: Detectors, fusion, policy
sections.explanation: Enabled detectors run on the shared `AnalysisContext`, `fuse` combines their results into one risk and category, and `decide` maps that to a decision, also considering extraction errors and whether an image was present. Reasons combine policy reasons, fusion notes and the top evidence from detectors with risk of at least 0.3. A clean ALLOW gets an explanatory reason listing which text was found.

sections.title: Report and audit
sections.explanation: Builds the `ScanReport` with the decision, risk, category (only when not ALLOW), reasons, detector results, segments, timings, fail-safe flag and image hash. The audit log write ignores `OSError`, so a logging failure never breaks a scan.

sections.title: One-line summary
sections.explanation: `summarize` formats a report as a single line with the decision, risk, category and a short snippet of each extracted segment, which is useful for logs and command-line tools.

guard/schemas.py.overview: This file holds the shared data vocabulary for the whole Threat Guard engine: the `Decision` and `Trust` enums plus the `TextSegment`, `DetectorResult`, and `ScanReport` dataclasses. It has the highest fan-in in the codebase, because ingress, extraction, every detector, fusion, policy, and the Virodh gateway all exchange these types. Tour Step 4 presents it as the contract that keeps every component in agreement.

sections.title: Decision and Trust enums
sections.explanation: `Decision` lists the three possible outcomes: ALLOW, REVIEW, and BLOCK. `Trust` sets up the instruction hierarchy. System text is trusted, the user's typed prompt is `USER`, and anything extracted from an image (OCR, QR, decoded) is `UNTRUSTED`. Both enums inherit from `str`, so they compare equal to plain strings and serialise to JSON without extra work. The `from __future__ import annotations` line lets the file use modern type hints such as `str | None`.

sections.title: TextSegment provenance record
sections.explanation: A `TextSegment` is a piece of text together with where it came from. It records the source, the trust level, the image view it was read from, the recovery method, the OCR confidence, a `parent` index for decoded children, and the ink `contrast`. The `recovered` property is True when reading the text meant undoing a transformation or when the text is nearly invisible, and detectors use that to rank evidence. `label()` builds a short human-readable origin such as `ocr via un-mirror`, which appears in reasons and in the console.

sections.title: DetectorResult evidence record
sections.explanation: Every detector returns a `DetectorResult` that holds a 0..1 risk score, its own confidence, human-readable evidence strings, and an optional attack category. The `status` and `error` fields let a failing detector report `error` instead of crashing the scan, and the policy layer then applies fail-safe rules. `field(default_factory=list)` gives each instance its own fresh list, which avoids Python's shared-mutable-default pitfall. The `engine` field records whether the finding came from the multimodal engine or the adversarial engine.

sections.title: ScanReport and serialisation
sections.explanation: `ScanReport` is the final output of one scan: the decision, the fused risk, the reasons, every detector result, every extracted segment, the per-stage timings, and whether a fail-safe fired. `to_dict()` uses `asdict` and then turns the enum values back into plain strings. `asdict` keeps Enum objects as they are, so without this step `json.dumps` would fail. The `hasattr` check keeps the conversion safe when a segment already holds a plain string.

virodh/inspector.py.overview: This file connects the Virodh gateway to the Threat Guard engine. It runs each inspection unit (a text chunk, or an image with its message text) through `ThreatGuard.scan`, and it guarantees bounded concurrency, a bounded queue, single-flight deduplication, a TTL/LRU result cache, and fail-closed behaviour. It then merges the per-unit reports into one `Inspection` and applies the adversarial-engine policy and the operator rules (blocked phrases and denied topics). Tour Step 4 describes it as the gateway-side orchestrator.

sections.title: Design guarantees and imports
sections.explanation: The module docstring lists the operational guarantees the rest of the file implements. A timed-out scan keeps its concurrency slot until its thread really finishes, so the thread pool is never oversubscribed. OCR is serialised inside each process, so throughput scales with the number of processes or replicas. `SEV` maps decisions to severity integers, which makes it easy to take the strictest decision and to sort units.

sections.title: Errors and result containers
sections.explanation: `Overloaded` carries a `retry_after` value, which the gateway turns into a 503 response with a Retry-After header. `InspectionTimeout` is raised when a scan runs too long. `UnitResult` pairs a unit with its `ScanReport`, the optional adversarial-engine result, and a cache flag. `Inspection` holds the request-level verdict, and it stores both the final `decision` and the raw `guard_decision` so that operator rules can be told apart from the guard's own findings.

sections.title: Evidence view for the console
sections.explanation: `evidence()` builds a trimmed, per-unit summary for the scan API and the admin console. It lists only untrusted segments under `found_in_image`, flags near-invisible text, caps the number and length of entries, and drops dotted timing keys (sub-stage timings). `_adv_dict` reduces an adversarial-engine result to its suspicious flag, risk, threshold, and the first few evidence strings.

sections.title: TTLCache with LRU eviction
sections.explanation: This is a small hand-written cache built on `OrderedDict`. Each entry stores an expiry time from `time.monotonic()`, and `move_to_end` marks recently used keys. An expired entry is deleted when it is read and counted as a miss. When the cache grows past `maxsize`, `popitem(last=False)` evicts the least recently used entry. The hit and miss counters feed `stats()`.

sections.title: Inspector setup and lifecycle
sections.explanation: The constructor reads the limits from the server config. It creates an `asyncio.Semaphore` and a scan thread pool of the same size, plus a smaller pool for the adversarial engine. The `ThreatGuard` engine is loaded lazily, and a guard can be injected, which the tests use to pass in fake engines. `cfg_hash` is a short hash of the guard config that becomes part of the cache key, so changing thresholds invalidates earlier verdicts. `warmup()` loads OCR and the adversarial model before traffic arrives and reports failures without raising.

sections.title: Scanning one unit synchronously
sections.explanation: `_scan_sync` runs in a worker thread. It starts the optional adversarial scan in the second pool, so that scan overlaps with the main `g.scan` call. An `IngressError` from the guard is allowed to propagate so that a bad image becomes a 400 response. An adversarial-engine failure is only recorded as an error name, so this optional engine can never block a request by failing.

sections.title: Admission control and slot release
sections.explanation: `_acquire` rejects the request right away with `Overloaded` when the semaphore is full and the queue is at capacity. Otherwise it waits for a slot, up to `queue_timeout`, and keeps the queue gauges up to date. `_run` registers `_release` as a done-callback on the executor future, so the slot is freed when the thread finishes, not when the caller gives up. `asyncio.shield` keeps the timeout from cancelling the underlying future, and a timeout surfaces as `InspectionTimeout`.

sections.title: Cache, single-flight, and fail-safe caching
sections.explanation: The cache key is a hash of the config hash, the adversarial flag, the image SHA-256, and the text. The method first checks the cache. It then checks `inflight`: when an identical unit is already being scanned, the caller awaits the same shared future (single-flight). On a miss it creates a future, and the no-op done-callback stops asyncio from warning that an exception was never retrieved. Results where a fail-safe fired are deliberately not cached, so a classifier outage is never remembered as a verdict.

sections.title: Merging units into a request verdict
sections.explanation: `inspect` scans all units concurrently with `asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` and then re-raises the first error it finds, so any failure means the request is not forwarded (fail closed). It ranks units by severity and then by risk, and the strictest unit sets the guard decision. Reasons are collected from every non-ALLOW unit and prefixed with the unit label when there are several units. If every unit was allowed, the reasons come from an image unit when one exists.

sections.title: Adversarial and operator rules
sections.explanation: A suspicious adversarial-engine result can only raise ALLOW to REVIEW, and only when the policy says `enforce`. Operator phrase rules are matched against the typed text and also against the text recovered from images. Denied topics are checked with the classifier in a thread, under a timeout. If that check fails, the inspection is marked fail-safe and ALLOW becomes REVIEW. Each operator hit can only make the decision stricter, which is enforced by comparing `SEV` values. `_adversarial` is a module-level helper so the thread pool can run it.

guard/extract/decoders.py.overview: This file recovers text that an attacker has hidden with an encoding trick: base64 (including base64 that OCR has partly misread), reversed text, ROT13, and MML-style word-substitution keys supplied in the prompt. The extraction pipeline calls these functions on OCR and QR segments, and every result becomes an untrusted `decoded` segment. Tour Step 5 lists these decoders as the last step of visual extraction.

sections.title: Patterns and OCR confusables
sections.explanation: `_B64` finds base64-alphabet runs of at least 12 characters with lookaround boundaries. `_B64_RUN` has no boundaries and is used on whitespace-joined text. `_DICT` and `_LIST` find bracketed literals that may hold a word-map key. The `_CONFUSABLE` table lists characters that OCR often mixes up (l/I/1, O/0, S/5, and so on), so the decoder can try plausible corrections.

sections.title: Robust base64 decoding
sections.explanation: Base64 decodes in independent 4-character quanta, so `_robust_b64` decodes each quantum on its own. It tries the confusable-character variants of each quantum (capped at 64) and keeps the variant whose bytes look most like text, as scored by `_quantum_score`, which rewards printable and alphabetic bytes. This means a single misread character only damages a few bytes instead of the whole payload. Padding is added first so the token length is a multiple of four.

sections.title: Finding and filtering base64 tokens
sections.explanation: `decode_base64_tokens` collects candidates from the raw text and from a version with all whitespace removed, because OCR splits long runs across lines. To avoid false positives, it keeps only tokens that contain a digit or one of + / =, since ordinary long words also match the base64 alphabet. A decoded result must be at least 90% clean ASCII, and `_looks_like_text` then requires at least two real words of three or more letters with good readability. Longer tokens are tried first, and results contained in an earlier result are skipped.

sections.title: Reverse and ROT13 checks
sections.explanation: Both functions apply their transform and return the result only when its readability score beats the original by more than 0.3. The margin keeps the functions from treating ordinary text as encoded.

sections.title: Word-map and word-list parsing
sections.explanation: In MML-style attacks the prompt carries a Python dict or list that explains how to un-scramble the words shown in the image. These helpers parse such literals with `ast.literal_eval`, which accepts only literals and never runs code. Each result is validated: a non-empty dict of strings, or a list of at least two strings.

sections.title: Applying the word map
sections.explanation: `apply_word_map` works out the mapping direction by counting which side, the keys or the values, actually appears in the text. The docstring notes that the attack's description and its real dict disagree on direction. It replaces longer keys first, so overlapping words substitute correctly, and uses case-insensitive whole-word regexes. It returns the rewritten text and the replacement count, and the pipeline only emits a segment when the count is above zero.

guard/extract/ocr.py.overview: This file wraps RapidOCR (an ONNX model running on the CPU) to read text from images, and it measures each line's ink contrast so the guard can spot near-invisible text. The extraction pipeline calls it on the original image and again on the mirrored, rotated, and contrast-boosted views. Tour Step 5 mentions OCR with RapidOCR on the CPU as the core of visual extraction.

sections.title: Lazy, thread-safe engine
sections.explanation: The RapidOCR engine is created on first use with double-checked locking, so it is built only once even when several threads ask for it at the same time. The import happens inside the function, which keeps module import cheap. The `VIRODH_OCR_THREADS` environment variable limits ONNX Runtime's intra-op threads, because by default each worker process would use every core and several workers would oversubscribe the CPU.

sections.title: OCR result dataclasses
sections.explanation: `OCRLine` stores the recognised text, the model's confidence, and a 0..1 contrast value. `OCRResult` joins the lines with newlines and computes their mean confidence, returning 0 when there are no lines so that an empty image does not cause a division by zero.

sections.title: Per-line contrast measurement
sections.explanation: The line's bounding box is clamped to the image and cropped from a grayscale copy. Contrast is the gap between the 3rd and 97th intensity percentiles, divided by 255. Using percentiles instead of min/max makes the value robust to stray noisy pixels. A low value means text a person can barely see, even though OCR can read it.

sections.title: Reading text
sections.explanation: `read_text` runs the engine on an RGB array while holding the module lock, so OCR is serialised within the process. That matches the inspector's note that CPU throughput scales with processes, not threads. Lines below `min_confidence` are dropped, and the rest are passed through `fix_spacing` and given a contrast value. `is_available()` is a health probe used during warmup.

guard/extract/pipeline.py.overview: This file is the visual extraction pipeline. Its job is to make every piece of text the target model could read visible to the guard as well. It runs QR decoding, OCR, orientation recovery, a faint-text pass, and the decoders in order, times each stage, and records failures instead of skipping them silently. The output is an `ExtractionResult` of segments that the detectors analyse, as described in Tour Step 5.

sections.title: Stages and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring lists the five extraction steps. `ExtractionResult` holds the segments together with per-stage timings, per-stage errors, and the list of image views tried, all of which end up in the scan report for transparency.

sections.title: Detecting genuinely new lines
sections.explanation: `_new_lines` keeps only the lines from the contrast-boosted pass that were not already read in the base OCR. It normalises text to lowercase alphanumerics and drops short lines, exact substrings, and near-duplicates (a `difflib` similarity above 0.8). This means only text that was truly hidden gets flagged.

sections.title: Setup, timing, QR and base OCR
sections.explanation: The user's prompt is always the first segment (index 0, `Trust.USER`). Text-only requests return at this point. The `timed` helper records each stage's duration, catches its exceptions into `res.errors`, and leaves the meaning of a failure to the policy engine. QR codes are decoded from the full-resolution image, while OCR runs on the model-resolution view, which is what the target model will see. Lines whose contrast is below `low_contrast_max` are also emitted as a separate `low_contrast` segment.

sections.title: Orientation recovery
sections.explanation: Other views are tried only when the base text looks unreadable (low readability and low confidence, and not valid base64) or when the prompt hints at mirroring or rotation. The order of views changes with the hint, so rotation hints try `rot180` first. A view is accepted when it is clearly more readable. When the prompt itself hinted at the trick, an equally readable view is also accepted. The loop stops early once readability reaches 0.8.

sections.title: Faint-text pass
sections.explanation: This pass runs only on document-like images, meaning a high white ratio and enough isolated light-ink pixels, and only when no low-contrast text has been found yet. The cost of the extra OCR call is the reason for these conditions. The image is contrast-boosted and read again, and only new lines are kept, tagged with `contrast_boost` and a contrast of 0.

sections.title: Decoder pass
sections.explanation: The decoders run over a snapshot of the OCR and QR segments (`n` is fixed before the loop starts), so new decoded segments are not decoded again. Each decoded child records its `parent` index and inherits its parent's view. The composite detector later uses that link to prefer the decoded text over the garbled original. A word list from the prompt is added as a `USER`-trust segment, because it came from the prompt, not from the image.

guard/extract/qr.py.overview: This file decodes QR codes with OpenCV. If the first attempt finds nothing, it retries on an upscaled copy and on an Otsu-binarised copy so that small or noisy codes are still read. The pipeline runs it first, on the full-resolution image, and every payload becomes an untrusted `qr` segment (Tour Step 5).

sections.title: Single decode attempt
sections.explanation: `_decode` tries `detectAndDecodeMulti` first, which handles several codes in one image, and falls back to the single-code `detectAndDecode`. OpenCV errors are caught and treated as finding nothing, so a malformed image cannot crash extraction.

sections.title: Retry strategy
sections.explanation: The image is converted to the BGR layout OpenCV expects. Images smaller than 1200 px get a 2x nearest-neighbour upscale, which keeps the module edges sharp, and every image also gets an Otsu-thresholded black-and-white copy. The attempts are tried in order and the loop stops at the first one that finds anything. Payloads are de-duplicated while keeping their order.

guard/ingress.py.overview: This file is the first stage of the guard: input validation. It enforces the prompt-length, byte-size, pixel, and format limits, re-decodes the image to strip metadata, builds the downscaled view that the model will see, and hashes the original bytes with SHA-256. Tour Step 5 describes it as the gate that runs before any analysis.

sections.title: Error type and validated input
sections.explanation: `IngressError` subclasses `ValueError` and carries a machine-readable `code`, which the gateway maps to a 400 response. `ValidatedInput` keeps two images: `image_full` is used for QR decoding at full resolution, and `image_model` is the downscaled view used for OCR because it matches what the target model receives.

sections.title: Validation and normalisation
sections.explanation: Null bytes are removed from the prompt and its length is checked. Image bytes are size-checked before they are decoded. Setting `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` makes Pillow raise `DecompressionBombError` for oversized images. A probe image is checked with `verify()`, and since `verify()` leaves that object unusable, the image is opened again. The format must be on the allowlist. Converting to RGB re-decodes the pixels and drops EXIF and other metadata. Animated images produce a warning, because only the first frame is inspected.

sections.title: PNG helper
sections.explanation: `to_png_bytes` re-encodes a PIL image to PNG in memory. Re-encoding means the bytes sent on contain only clean pixel data.

guard/detectors/base.py.overview: This file defines the plugin interface that every threat detector implements, together with the `AnalysisContext` that detectors share. As the module docstring says, detectors only report evidence and never decide ALLOW, REVIEW, or BLOCK; fusion and policy make that decision later. Tour Step 6 introduces it as the shared Detector interface.

sections.title: AnalysisContext
sections.explanation: The context bundles the validated input, the extraction result, and the config. It also carries the results of the hosted-classifier calls, which are made once and shared: `item_ids` maps classifier item ids to segment indices (with -1 for the composite item), `verdicts` holds the policy-classifier output, and `pg_scores` holds the Prompt Guard score for each segment. Each of these has an error field. Calling the classifiers once and sharing the results avoids duplicate network calls across detectors. `untrusted()` returns the image-derived segments together with their indices.

sections.title: Snippet helper
sections.explanation: `snippet` collapses whitespace and truncates text with an ellipsis. Detectors use it so that evidence strings stay short and readable.

sections.title: Detector abstract base class
sections.explanation: `run()` is a template method. It times `analyse()`, turns any exception into a `DetectorResult` with `status="error"`, and sets the detector name. Because of this, one failing detector cannot take down the scan, and the policy layer can apply fail-safe rules to the error status. Subclasses only implement the abstract `analyse()`.

guard/detectors/composite.py.overview: This file is the cross-modal consistency detector. It catches multimodal requests that are split so that the prompt and the image text each look benign, while their combination is harmful. It builds a composite text from the prompt and the best readable image text, reads the classifier's verdict on that combination, and reports whether the harm only appears when the two are put together (Tour Step 6).

sections.title: Deferral phrases
sections.explanation: `DEFERRAL` is a case-insensitive regex for prompts that hand the real task off to the image (for example asking to complete the list in the image or to follow its steps). On its own it does not change the risk score. It only adds supporting evidence and a detail flag.

sections.title: Building the composite text
sections.explanation: `build_composite` lists every untrusted segment with its origin label. It skips a raw original OCR segment when a decoded child of it exists, so the classifier sees the readable version instead of the garbled one. Any word list given in the prompt is appended. The prompt is capped at 900 characters and each image part at 600, which bounds the size of the classifier input.

sections.title: Scoring the combined request
sections.explanation: The detector is skipped when there was no image text to combine. It raises an error when the classifier is unavailable, and `Detector.run` turns that into an error status that triggers the fail-safe rules. When the composite verdict is harmful, the evidence wording depends on whether any single part was also harmful. If no part was harmful on its own, the finding is labelled a cross-modal split request, the case this detector exists to catch. Risk equals the classifier's confidence.

guard/detectors/harm.py.overview: This file is the harmful-content detector. It asks whether any single piece of text, either the prompt or text taken from the image, is a harmful request according to the shared policy-classifier verdicts. It turns those verdicts into evidence and a risk score, and leaves the combined request to the composite detector (Tour Step 6).

sections.title: Per-segment harm evidence
sections.explanation: The detector raises an error when the classifier verdicts are missing, so that the fail-safe path is taken instead of an empty result being read as safe. It loops over the classifier items, skips the composite item (index below 0), and records evidence for each harmful verdict. The highest-confidence verdict sets the risk, and the category says whether the harm was in the prompt (index 0) or in the image. When nothing harmful is found, confidence falls back to 0.8.

guard/detectors/injection.py.overview: This file is the instruction-hierarchy and jailbreak-intent detector. Its rule is that text taken from an image is data, so image text that gives commands to the AI counts as an injection. It combines regex patterns aimed at the AI, the policy classifier's `instruction_to_ai` flag, Llama Prompt Guard scores, and a hidden-text cue. It also gives a lower weight to jailbreak framing in the user's own prompt (Tour Step 6).

sections.title: AI-directed pattern table
sections.explanation: `AI_DIRECTED` is a list of compiled regexes, each with a weight and a human-readable reason. They cover requests to ignore instructions, text posing as a system or admin message, commands addressed to an AI or reviewer, dictated exact output, and announced new instructions. `_ADDRESSEE` is shared between the patterns, and matching is case-insensitive. The weights act as the pattern's risk contribution.

sections.title: Hidden-text cue and prompt framing
sections.explanation: `INSTRUCTION_CUE` is a much broader instruction-like regex, and it is applied only to text recovered with a hidden method (low contrast or contrast boost). The comment gives the reason: legitimate documents do not hide instructions from the people reading them. `JAILBREAK_FRAMING` scores the user's own prompt for role-play or no-limits framing and for deferring the task to the image, with lower weights.

sections.title: Pattern scoring helper
sections.explanation: `_patterns` collapses whitespace first, so that an OCR line break cannot split a phrase and hide it. It returns the maximum weight among the matching patterns and the list of reasons.

sections.title: Scoring untrusted segments
sections.explanation: For each untrusted segment the detector combines the pattern score, the classifier score, Prompt Guard, and the hidden-text signal, and takes the maximum. Prompt Guard is halved unless a pattern or the classifier agrees, because on its own it fires on harmless notices. Each evidence item is stored with its recovered flag and risk, then sorted so that recovered or hidden text and the strongest findings come first. The highest-risk segment sets the category.

sections.title: Prompt framing and result
sections.explanation: The user's prompt (segment 0) is scored separately: the higher of the framing patterns and 0.6 times its Prompt Guard score. It overrides the result only when it is higher than every image-side risk. At the top of `analyse`, the detector raises an error only when both classifier sources are missing, so it degrades gracefully when one is unavailable. The raw Prompt Guard scores are kept in `details` for debugging.

guard/detectors/obfuscation.py.overview: This file is a deterministic detector that makes no API calls. It flags signs that text was deliberately hidden from people or from simple filters, such as low contrast, mirroring or rotation, encodings, word maps, and empty numbered scaffolds. Hiding text is not an attack on its own (mirrored AMBULANCE signs are an example), so fusion only lets this score amplify risk that other detectors found (Tour Steps 6 and 7).

sections.title: Signals and method weights
sections.explanation: `SCAFFOLD` matches image text that ends with an empty 1./2./3. list waiting to be filled in. `DECODE_HINT` matches prompts that explain how to transform the image. `METHOD_WEIGHTS` gives each extraction method recorded on a segment a weight and a message template. Methods that hide text from people (low contrast, contrast boost) carry the highest weights, and sideways rotation carries the lowest.

sections.title: Collecting and combining signals
sections.explanation: The detector reads the `method` of each segment, checks the original OCR for a scaffold, and flags long QR payloads that are free text instead of a URL, Wi-Fi config, mailto, tel, or vCard. A decode hint in the prompt adds one more signal. The weights are combined with noisy-OR (1 minus the product of 1 minus each weight), so several independent signals raise the risk without ever going past 1. The technique names are taken from the message prefixes to build the category, and confidence is fixed at 0.9 because the signals are deterministic.

guard/fusion.py.overview: Combines the per-detector results from Step 6 into a single risk score, an attack category, and a list of notes. It is a pure function with no I/O: it gets a dict of `DetectorResult` objects and the guard config, and returns `(risk, category, notes)` for the policy engine in `guard/policy.py` to act on. The docstring gives the formula. Overlapping content detectors are merged with `max`, independent signals with noisy-OR, and obfuscation can only amplify risk that already exists.

sections.title: Fusion design notes
sections.explanation: The module docstring is the specification for the whole file. `harm` and `composite` use the same classifier, so their evidence overlaps and summing them would count it twice. They are merged with `max`. Injection is an independent signal, so it is combined with that content score using noisy-OR. The docstring also says failed detectors are *excluded* here on purpose, because deciding what a failure means belongs to the policy engine.

sections.title: Effective detector score
sections.explanation: `_eff` turns one detector result into a score clamped to [0, 1]. A missing result, or one whose `status` is not `ok`, contributes 0. Otherwise the score is `weight * risk_score * max(0.5, confidence)`. Confidence has a floor of 0.5, so a low-confidence detector is discounted by at most half rather than silenced.

sections.title: Core risk formula
sections.explanation: Weights come from `cfg['detectors'][name]['weight']`. Obfuscation defaults to 0.6, the others to 1.0. `core = 1 - (1-inj)(1-content)` is noisy-OR. Obfuscation then closes part of the remaining gap to 1, scaled by `min(1, core/0.3)`, so it has little effect when core risk is near zero. The final `max(risk, 0.25 * obf)` keeps obfuscation visible on its own, but at most 0.25, which (per the comment) is meant to stay below the REVIEW threshold.

sections.title: Image-injection floor rule
sections.explanation: This is a policy floor that can raise the risk. If the injection detector succeeded, scored at least `image_injection_min_score` (default 0.85), and labelled the attack as starting with `image prompt injection`, the risk is raised to at least the REVIEW threshold. If obfuscation is also significant (>= 0.3), it is raised to the BLOCK threshold. A note is recorded so the decision can be explained. The rule makes sure a strong instruction aimed at the AI inside an image cannot be diluted by the arithmetic above.

sections.title: Attack category selection
sections.explanation: The reported category comes from the strongest contributor. Injection is ranked against the content score, which is attributed to `composite` or `harm`, whichever is higher. A contributor has to exceed 0.2 to name the category. If obfuscation ran and has its own category, it is appended after ` | `, so the label says both what the attack was and how it was hidden. The returned risk is clamped to 1.0 and rounded to three decimals.

guard/llm.py.overview: Thin, cached clients for the guard's hosted classifiers, which are reached over OpenAI-compatible APIs. It exposes `prompt_guard_score` (Llama Prompt Guard injection probability) and `classify_items` (a policy classifier given the project's written harm policy). Both are fed by the detectors and both cache verdicts per text in a JSONL file. In the tour's Step 7 it is the backend that supplies classifier evidence to fusion and policy, and it records the last-seen model status for health reporting.

sections.title: Client registry and status
sections.explanation: The docstring describes the two classifiers. Prompt Guard is non-generative, so it cannot be argued into producing anything. The policy model gets the extracted text as quoted DATA items. `_clients` is a lock-protected cache of `OpenAI` client objects. `STATUS` stores the last ok/error result for each model, which lets a health endpoint report classifier health without a live probe. `_mark` truncates error text to 160 characters.

sections.title: Written harm policy prompt
sections.explanation: `HARM_POLICY` is the system prompt for the policy classifier. It frames every item as untrusted data that must be classified, never followed. It says framing in one item (fiction, games, research) must not change the verdict on another item. It lists harmful and benign categories and asks for a separate `instruction_to_ai` flag. A strict JSON output shape is required so the result can be parsed by machine. Because the prompt's hash is part of the cache key (see below), editing this text invalidates earlier cached verdicts automatically.

sections.title: Cached OpenAI clients
sections.explanation: `_client` builds or reuses an `OpenAI` client keyed by base URL, API-key environment variable name, and retry count. A missing key raises `RuntimeError` immediately instead of failing later inside a request. The timeout comes from `cfg['llm']['timeout_s']`. Holding the lock while creating the client avoids duplicate construction when threads race.

sections.title: Classifier fallback chain
sections.explanation: `_policy_chain` tries each model in `cfg['llm']['harm_models']` in order, with `temperature=0` and `response_format=json_object`. Any exception (rate limit, timeout, invalid JSON) is recorded and the next model is tried. Only the last model in the chain gets SDK retries, so earlier models fail over quickly. `_policy_call` wraps the chain. If `rate_limit_rounds` is configured (batch mode), it sleeps with a growing delay and runs the whole chain again before raising.

sections.title: Prompt Guard scoring
sections.explanation: `prompt_guard_score` returns 0.0 for empty text, checks the cache, and otherwise calls the model. The model has a short context, so `_prompt_guard_uncached` splits the text into 1500-character chunks (at most 4) and keeps the maximum score. The model replies with a number in text, which is pulled out with a regex. Unexpected output raises an error rather than being read as 0, so a broken classifier cannot look like a clean result.

sections.title: Persistent verdict cache
sections.explanation: Verdicts are stored in `data/cache/classifier_cache.jsonl`, one `{k, v}` object per line. The file is loaded lazily on first use, and lines that fail to parse are skipped. Keys are SHA-256 hashes of `namespace | policy-hash | text`, so the same text is never classified twice under the same policy. Writes append to the file under a lock, which is simple and crash-tolerant, though the file only ever grows.

sections.title: Batch item classification
sections.explanation: `classify_items` serves cached items directly and sends all uncached ones to the policy model in a single call. Each item is wrapped in `<<< >>>` delimiters with an `ITEM id:` label and truncated to 1500 characters. If the model leaves items out, `_classify_uncached` asks again once for just the missing ones. Items still missing after that raise `ValueError`, which keeps the system fail-safe because the policy engine treats a failed detector as grounds for at least REVIEW.

sections.title: Defensive response parsing
sections.explanation: `_parse` normalises the model's JSON into fixed fields: booleans, a category of at most 40 characters, confidence clamped to [0, 1], and a reason of at most 160 characters. It handles one known failure: if the model renamed the IDs but returned the right number of rows, rows are matched to items by position. Non-dict rows are ignored, so malformed output degrades to 'missing items' instead of crashing.

guard/policy.py.overview: The guard's policy engine, and according to its docstring the only place where a fused risk score becomes ALLOW, REVIEW, or BLOCK. It applies profile-adjusted thresholds, enforces fail-safe rules when required inspection steps or detectors failed, and combines the main decision with the optional adversarial-image engine. It is the second half of tour Step 7, using the risk produced by `guard/fusion.py`.

sections.title: Profiles and required steps
sections.explanation: `PROFILES` maps a profile name to a multiplier on the thresholds: `balanced` is 1.0 and `strict` is 0.8. `decide` later clamps the multiplier with `min(1.0, ...)`, which is how profiles can only tighten the thresholds and never loosen them. `REQUIRED_EXTRACTION` names QR and OCR as the extraction steps whose failure triggers fail-safe handling when an image is present.

sections.title: Threshold decision and fail-safe
sections.explanation: The REVIEW and BLOCK thresholds are scaled by the profile factor, and the risk is compared against them. Two kinds of failure are then collected: required extraction errors, which only count when there is an image, and any enabled detector marked `required` that is missing or has `status == 'error'`. If anything failed, `fail_safe` is set, the reasons are prefixed with `fail-safe:`, and an ALLOW is raised to REVIEW. An image that was not fully inspected therefore never goes through on ALLOW.

sections.title: Combining the adversarial engine
sections.explanation: `combine_engines` merges in the result of the separate adversarial-image engine. That engine is optional and does not trigger fail-safe: if there is no report, or the report is not suspicious, the decision is unchanged. When it is suspicious, a reason labelled `[adversarial engine]` is built from up to two pieces of evidence. An ALLOW becomes REVIEW, or BLOCK only if `adversarial.can_block` is set. Decisions that are already stricter keep their level and just gain the reason.

guard/envelope.py.overview: A very small module that wraps a forwarded user prompt in a security preamble, inspired by AdaShield-S. The preamble tells the downstream model that the attached image is untrusted and that any text or instructions in it are content to describe, not commands to follow. The docstring says this is an extra layer applied to every forwarded request, on top of the guard's decision, and never a replacement for it.

sections.title: Purpose and preamble text
sections.explanation: `PREAMBLE` is a fixed string labelled as a security notice from the application. It marks image content (text, QR codes, instructions) as untrusted and states that only the user's request is the task. It ends with `User request: ` so the real prompt follows directly. Keeping the text constant makes the defence predictable and easy to audit.

sections.title: wrap_prompt helper
sections.explanation: `wrap_prompt` just puts the preamble in front of the prompt. It is a plain function so callers (for example the gateway's upstream payload builder, which per-key policies can switch with an `envelope` flag) can apply it without depending on anything else. The user's prompt is not escaped or changed.

guard/output_guard.py.overview: Checks the model's reply after the request was forwarded (an ECSO-inspired output check). It looks for markers, meaning code words or quoted phrases, that appeared only in untrusted image text. If the reply outputs one of them, the model may have followed a hidden instruction. The important part is telling real compliance apart from a reply that merely quotes, reports, or refuses the hidden text. The same `complied()` function is used by the evaluation code, so attack success is measured the same way in tests and in production.

sections.title: Marker and context patterns
sections.explanation: `CODE` matches code-word markers such as uppercase letters, a hyphen and digits. `QUOTED` captures quoted phrases of 6-60 characters. `REPORTING_BEFORE` looks for a reporting verb ('says', 'asks', 'wants me to') close before the marker. `REFUSAL` detects explicit refusals such as 'will not follow' or 'ignoring the hidden instruction'. `QUOTE_SPAN` finds short quoted spans. The comment notes that plain apostrophes are not used as delimiters because they appear inside words.

sections.title: Markdown stripping
sections.explanation: `_plain` removes bold, italic, code, blockquote, and strikethrough markers before matching. Without this, a reply like 'I will **not** follow' would not match the refusal regex.

sections.title: Compliance vs. mention
sections.explanation: `complied` returns False straight away if the marker is not in the reply, or if the reply contains an explicit refusal. Otherwise it collects the 'payload words' of the injected sentence and checks each occurrence of the marker. The occurrence counts as quoted if at least 60% of the payload words appear nearby, as reported if a reporting verb comes before it, and as a mention if the marker is directly inside quotes or inside a short quoted span. One occurrence that is none of these is enough to count as compliance. As the docstring says, admitting the override and still outputting the marker is compliance.

sections.title: check_reply entry point
sections.explanation: `check_reply` takes the user's prompt from the first segment and the untrusted segments from the `ScanReport`. It collects candidate markers from that untrusted text and discards any that also appear in the user's own prompt, because a marker must come from the image to be meaningful. It returns `(ok, reasons)`, with one human-readable reason for each marker the reply obeyed.

virodh/upstream.py.overview: Forwards allowed requests to the real model providers. Each worker keeps one pooled `httpx.AsyncClient`. Each named upstream has a circuit breaker that stops sending traffic to a failing provider. A deterministic offline `mock` upstream supports demos and load tests without provider quota. In tour Step 8 this is the forwarding step between the guard's decision and the output guard. It also reports Prometheus metrics through `virodh/metrics.py`.

sections.title: Reply type and exception
sections.explanation: `UpstreamReply` is a dataclass holding the HTTP status, the parsed JSON (or None), the raw text, the latency in ms, and an optional `retry_after` header so the gateway can pass the provider's back-off hint on to the client. `CircuitOpen` carries the upstream name and how long until it can be retried.

sections.title: Per-upstream circuit breaker
sections.explanation: `Breaker` counts consecutive failures for each upstream name. When the count reaches the limit, it opens for `cooldown` seconds (measured on the monotonic clock) and sets a gauge. It then sets the counter to `limit - 1`, which makes it half-open: the next failure re-opens it immediately, and a success (`ok`) resets it and clears the gauge. The docstring notes that 429 responses do not open the breaker because they mean quota, not an outage. `state()` reports which breakers are open for the admin system view.

sections.title: Pooled client and model specs
sections.explanation: `Upstreams` builds a single `AsyncClient` with separate connect, read, write, and pool timeouts and connection-pool limits from the server config. Redirects are disabled, a sensible default for a proxy. An optional `transport` argument lets tests inject a mock transport. `spec()` resolves a public model ID to its upstream configuration, and `available()` reports whether that upstream can be used (mock, or its API-key environment variable is set).

sections.title: Forwarding with retry
sections.explanation: `chat` sends mock models to `_mock_reply`, checks the breaker, and returns 503 if the provider key is not configured. Connection errors are retried once, because the request never reached the provider and so cannot have run twice. Timeouts and other HTTP errors fail immediately with 504 or 502, record a breaker failure, and increment a counter. Once a response arrives, 5xx counts as a breaker failure and anything below 400 counts as a success. The body is parsed as JSON if possible, and the raw text is truncated to 2000 characters.

sections.title: Offline mock model
sections.explanation: `_ms` gives the elapsed milliseconds. `_mock_reply` builds a deterministic Chat Completions response that echoes the last user text and the number of images received, with rough token counts (characters divided by 4). It never makes a network call, so the whole gateway pipeline can be tested end to end offline.

virodh/admin.py.overview: The FastAPI router behind `/admin/api/*`, which the console and the Node dashboard use. It exposes overview and system status, model listing, API-key and policy CRUD, the request log, usage statistics, and a playground that runs the same pipeline as `/v1/chat/completions`. Every route depends on `require_admin`, which defers to `virodh/security.py`. In tour Step 9 it is the operator-facing surface over `store.py` and `policy.py`.

sections.title: Router setup and admin guard
sections.explanation: The docstring describes access control: a CSRF header plus either an admin token or a loopback client. `require_admin` calls `admin_denied` and turns a denial into a 401 or 403 `HTTPException`. `ADMIN = [Depends(require_admin)]` is reused on every route. `_REFUSAL` is a heuristic regex used later to label unguarded demo replies as refusals. `_bad` is a helper that raises a structured 4xx error.

sections.title: Overview, system, models
