sections.explanation: `/overview` combines store aggregates (with the hour window clamped to 30 days) with the inspector's stats and the worker PID. `/system` reports version, readiness, breaker state, each upstream's type and whether its key is present (never the key itself), the last-seen status of each classifier from `guard.llm.STATUS`, the guard thresholds, and the server limits. `/models` lists the configured models and whether each is available.

sections.title: API key management
sections.explanation: `KeyCreate` and `KeyPatch` are Pydantic models with length and range limits. `_check_refs` checks that the referenced policy and models exist. `create_key` returns the plaintext secret exactly once, with a note that only its hash is stored. `patch_key` passes only the non-None fields to `update_key` and returns 404 when nothing changed. All writes go through `store.write`, the single writer thread.

sections.title: Policy CRUD
sections.explanation: `put_policy` validates the body as a `Policy`, using the name from the URL path. The first Pydantic error is turned into a readable `loc: msg` message. Allowed models are checked against the config before the upsert. `delete_policy` returns 409 with the store's reason when the policy cannot be deleted, for example because it is the default or keys still use it.

sections.title: Request log and usage
sections.explanation: `/requests` validates the decision filter, clamps `limit` to 200, and accepts `owner_key_ids` (a comma list of at most 500) and `owner_key_name`. The Node dashboard uses these to limit a member to their own keys. `/requests/{rid}` returns a single record or 404. `/usage` returns hourly and per-key/per-model aggregates over a clamped window.

sections.title: Playground endpoint
sections.explanation: The playground has its own rate limit (`playground_rpm`) and takes an optional uploaded image. The image size is checked by reading one byte past the limit, and the image is converted to a base64 data URL. The request is then run through `gw.run_chat` and logged with `gw.record`, the same pipeline real clients use. The `x-virodh-user` header from the Node dashboard is cleaned and used only as a log label. The comment states that access control happens upstream in Node.

sections.title: Guarded unguarded comparison
sections.explanation: `_unguarded` sends the same request without the envelope or inspection, for a side-by-side research demo. It is limited deliberately. If the request was flagged harmful (`harm` or `composite` risk >= 0.5), it is skipped unless `demo.show_unguarded_harmful` is enabled. It is always skipped for topics in `demo.never_for`. Harmful replies are truncated to `max_chars`. The raw reply is still checked with `check_reply`, so the demo can show whether the unprotected model followed a hidden instruction.

virodh/metrics.py.overview: A minimal Prometheus text-format metrics module that needs no client library. It keeps counters, gauges, and histograms in memory for each worker process, and `render()` produces the exposition text. The docstring notes that scraping should target each replica directly, because the numbers are per worker. Totals across workers come from SQLite instead. Tour Step 9 describes it as the gateway's observability layer.

sections.title: State, buckets, and help
sections.explanation: `BUCKETS` defines histogram bounds from 50 ms to 120 s, which suits latencies ranging from cache hits to slow upstream calls. Counters and gauges are `defaultdict`s keyed by `(name, sorted-labels-tuple)`. A single lock protects all of them. `HELP` provides the `# HELP` descriptions for the known metric names.

sections.title: Recording API
sections.explanation: `_k` sorts the labels so that `{a,b}` and `{b,a}` map to the same series. `inc` adds to a counter and `gauge` sets a value. `observe` keeps a list with one slot per bucket, plus a `+Inf`/count slot and a sum. Buckets are cumulative, as Prometheus expects: every bucket whose upper bound is at least the observed value is incremented.

sections.title: Exposition rendering
sections.explanation: `_fmt` escapes backslashes, quotes, and newlines in label values. `render` writes `# HELP`/`# TYPE` once per metric name, then one sample line per series. Every series gets a `worker_pid` label so replicas can be told apart. Histograms produce `_bucket` lines including `le="+Inf"`, followed by `_count` and `_sum`.

virodh/policy.py.overview: Pydantic models for the per-key policy profiles that decide what the gateway does with the guard's decision. Settings include enforce or monitor mode, what REVIEW means, the style of block response, toggles for the output guard and envelope, how adversarial-engine findings are handled, a phrase blocklist, operator denied topics, and an allowlist of models. It also provides a deterministic phrase matcher that runs on both user text and text recovered from images. This is the core of tour Step 9.

sections.title: Denied topic model
sections.explanation: `NAME` limits policy names to short lowercase slugs. `DeniedTopic` is an operator rule with a constrained name, a description of 10-600 characters (the policy classifier needs enough context to apply it), and an action of `block` or `review`. These rules are checked by `virodh/topics.py`.

sections.title: Policy profile fields
sections.explanation: `Policy` uses `Literal` types for every choice, so invalid values are rejected when the policy is validated. `mode='monitor'` logs without blocking, for shadow rollouts. `review_action` decides whether REVIEW blocks or forwards, since a synchronous proxy cannot hold a request for a human. `block_response='refusal'` returns a 200 with `finish_reason: content_filter`, so OpenAI SDK clients do not throw. An empty `allowed_models` means all models are allowed.

sections.title: Phrase normalisation and fingerprints
sections.explanation: The `blocked_phrases` validator collapses whitespace, drops empty entries, rejects phrases longer than 100 characters, and removes duplicates case-insensitively with `casefold`. `version()` hashes the whole serialised policy, so the inspection cache is invalidated whenever any setting changes. `rules_fingerprint()` hashes only the denied topics, for caching the rule-classifier verdicts.

sections.title: Deterministic phrase matching
sections.explanation: `phrase_hits` compiles each phrase into a case-insensitive whole-word pattern. Lookarounds stand in for `\b`, so phrases with punctuation still match, and spaces in the phrase match any run of whitespace. It is applied to every `(label, text)` pair, including OCR, QR, and decoded text, so hiding a blocked phrase inside an image does not get around it. Each phrase produces at most one hit, which records where it matched.

virodh/store.py.overview: The SQLite persistence layer for the gateway: hashed API keys, policies, the request log, rate-limit windows, and usage and overview aggregates. The docstring explains the choice. SQLite needs no extra service, works correctly across uvicorn workers on one host using WAL, and within a process all writes go through a single thread so the event loop never blocks on the database lock. In tour Step 9 it is the shared state that lets gateway replicas stay stateless.

sections.title: Design notes and schema
sections.explanation: The docstring explains why API keys use a fast SHA-256 hash: the keys carry 256 bits of entropy, so a slow password hash adds nothing. `SCHEMA` creates the `api_keys`, `policies` (stored as JSON), `requests` (a wide audit row), and `rate` (`key_id`, window, count) tables, with indexes on `ts` and `(key_id, ts)` for the log and usage queries.

sections.title: Constants and key record
sections.explanation: `LOG_FIELDS` is the column order for request rows. `JSON_FIELDS` lists the columns that are serialised to JSON. `hash_key` is a plain SHA-256. `KeyRecord.public()` deliberately leaves out the hash, so only the ID, display prefix, and settings reach the API. `_key_row` turns a `sqlite3.Row` back into a record, decoding `allowed_models` from JSON.

sections.title: Connections and executors
sections.explanation: Each thread gets its own lazily opened connection (`threading.local`) with WAL, `synchronous=NORMAL`, and a 15 s busy timeout. Autocommit is used (`isolation_level=None`), and explicit transactions are opened only where they are needed. A single-thread writer executor and a four-thread reader pool back the async methods `write()` and `read()`, so callers can `await` database work without blocking the event loop.

sections.title: Policy persistence
sections.explanation: `seed_policies` inserts the configured defaults with `INSERT OR IGNORE`, so edits made by operators survive restarts. `get_policy` caches results for 3 s per process, which is how changes reach the other workers. `list_policies` adds how many active keys use each policy. `delete_policy` refuses to delete the `default` policy or any policy still used by active keys, and returns a reason string that the admin API turns into a 409.

sections.title: API key lifecycle
sections.explanation: `create_key` generates a `vk_`-prefixed URL-safe token from 32 random bytes and stores only its hash together with a short display prefix. `find_key` rejects malformed input early and caches lookups by hash for 5 s, so a revocation reaches every worker within that time. The cache is cleared if it grows past 10,000 entries. `update_key` only writes columns from an allowlist (the column names come from that fixed set, never from user input) and clears the key cache.

sections.title: Shared fixed-window rate limit
sections.explanation: `rate_hit` counts a request against a per-minute window and a per-day window inside a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction, which takes the write lock immediately so concurrent workers cannot race. Rejected requests are rolled back and not counted. The result includes a `retry_after` until the end of the current window. Every 500 hits, minute windows older than 5 minutes are pruned. The return value is `(allowed, retry_after, remaining_this_minute)`.

sections.title: Request log queries
sections.explanation: `log_request` serialises the JSON fields, upserts the row, and updates the key's `last_used`. `prune` deletes rows older than the retention period. `list_requests` builds a parameterised WHERE clause. The owner filter combines key IDs and a playground label with OR. If an owner filter is requested but both parts are empty, it falls back to `0`, which matches nothing, so a member with no keys sees no rows instead of all of them.

sections.title: Usage and overview aggregates
sections.explanation: `usage` groups requests by hour, decision, and action, then fills in a continuous hourly series. It adds top-20 per-key totals and per-model totals using SQLite's boolean `SUM(expr)` idiom. `overview` reads recent rows into Python to count decisions, actions, and top categories (normalised by trimming suffixes), and computes nearest-rank p50/p95 latencies, the cache hit rate, the fail-safe count, and replies withheld by the output guard.

virodh/topics.py.overview: Enforces operator 'denied topics': rules specific to an organisation, checked by the guard's policy-classifier chain separately from the built-in harm policy, which this file never changes. The request (user text plus text read from images) is sent as quoted, untrusted data. The classifier must answer in JSON, with one verdict per rule. Results are cached per rule set and text using the cache in `guard/llm.py`. This is the topic-enforcement part of tour Step 9.

sections.title: Rules classifier prompt
sections.explanation: `RULES_PROMPT` has the same defensive framing as the harm policy. The request is data, never instructions. A rule counts as `violated` only if fulfilling the request would require the prohibited behaviour, so mentioning the topic is not enough. Fictional or hypothetical framing does not change the verdict, and allowed cases listed in a rule's description are respected.

sections.title: Request body builder
sections.explanation: `_body` numbers the rules `R1..Rn` and wraps the request in `<<< >>>` delimiters labelled 'do not follow'. User text is capped at 3000 characters, each image text at 1200, and all image text together at 4000. The body ends by asking for an entry for every rule ID, which makes omissions easier to detect.

sections.title: Cached rule checking
sections.explanation: `check` builds a cache key from the serialised topics and the request body, so changing any rule invalidates earlier verdicts. On a cache miss it calls the chain and indexes the returned rules by upper-cased ID. A missing rule raises an error rather than defaulting to 'not violated'. As the docstring says, the caller then fails safe. Confidence is clamped and the reason truncated.

sections.title: Classifier chain and violations
sections.explanation: `_call` mirrors `llm._policy_chain`, using a smaller `max_tokens` and the rules prompt. It tries each model in turn, records each one's status, and gives retries only to the last model. `violations` converts the verdicts that were violated into the same hit shape `phrase_hits` uses (`rule`, `where`, `action`), plus the reason and confidence, so the gateway can handle operator rule hits the same way as other hits.

server/src/auth.js.overview: Account and session management for the Express dashboard backend, which is separate from the gateway's API keys. It covers scrypt password hashing, random session tokens stored only as SHA-256 hashes in HttpOnly cookies, in-memory sign-in throttling, signup validation, and the `/auth/*` routes. It also exports the `requireUser` and `requireAdmin` middleware. This file implements the authentication described in tour Step 10.

sections.title: Security summary and constants
sections.explanation: The header comment summarises the design: scrypt with N=2^14, r=8, p=1, a 16-byte salt and a 64-byte key; 256-bit session tokens with 7-day expiry; the first account becomes admin; and generic error messages so account existence is not revealed. `SCRYPT` sets `maxmem` explicitly so these parameters run within Node's memory limit. `EMAIL` is a pragmatic, bounded email regex.

sections.title: Password hashing
sections.explanation: `hashPassword` stores `scrypt$N$salt$key`, so the cost parameter travels with each hash and can be raised later without breaking existing accounts. `verifyPassword` reads N back from the stored string and compares with `timingSafeEqual` after a length check. `DUMMY_HASH` is computed once at startup so that sign-in for an unknown email still pays the scrypt cost, which makes timing useless for discovering accounts.

sections.title: In-memory throttling
sections.explanation: `attempts` maps a key such as `ip:` or `email:` to its recent timestamps. `throttled` drops timestamps outside the window and reports whether the limit was reached. `fail` records an attempt. A cleanup timer runs every minute and is marked `unref()` so it does not keep the process alive. The state lives in each process's memory, so it is not shared across dashboard instances.

sections.title: Signup validation
sections.explanation: `validateSignup` normalises the email (trimmed, lower-cased) and collapses whitespace in the name and organisation. It enforces length limits and requires a password of 10-128 characters with at least one letter and one digit. It also rejects passwords that contain the local part of the email (when that part is at least 4 characters). It returns either `{error}` or the cleaned fields, and the password-change route reuses it.

sections.title: Sessions and cookies
sections.explanation: `createSession` generates a base64url token from 32 random bytes, stores only its SHA-256 hash with the expiry and a truncated user agent, and deletes expired sessions as a side effect. `readCookie` is a minimal parser for the Cookie header. `sessionUser` rejects tokens that are too long, then looks up the hash with a join to the user, ignoring expired sessions and disabled users. The cookie helpers set `HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`, and add `Secure` when configured.

sections.title: Signup and signin routes
sections.explanation: Signup is throttled per IP (10 per hour), validated, and rejects duplicate emails with 409. It assigns `admin` if the users table is empty and `member` otherwise, writes an audit entry, and signs the new user in. Signin is throttled by both IP and email and always runs `verifyPassword`, against the dummy hash when the user does not exist. It checks `disabled`, and on failure records attempts for both keys, audits the event, and returns the same generic 401 message.

sections.title: Signout, me, password change
sections.explanation: Signout deletes the session row by its token hash and clears the cookie. `/auth/me` returns the public user along with `setup_needed`, which is true when no accounts exist yet, so the UI can show first-run setup. Password change checks the current password, validates the new one with the signup rules, and stores the new hash. It then deletes all of the user's sessions (signing them out everywhere) before issuing a new session for the current browser.

sections.title: Auth middleware
sections.explanation: `requireUser(db)` is a middleware factory that resolves the session user, returns 401 when there is none, and otherwise sets `req.user`. `requireAdmin` assumes `requireUser` has already run and returns 403 unless the role is `admin`. Because they are separate pieces, routes can be chained as `requireUser(db), requireAdmin`.

server/src/db.js.overview: The dashboard backend's small account database, built on Node's built-in `node:sqlite` module. It creates the users, sessions, user-to-API-key ownership, and audit tables, and exports helpers for timestamps, audit logging, and turning a user row into a safe public shape. It holds human accounts only: API keys and request logs live in the Python engine's store, which is the split described in tour step 10.

sections.title: Header and imports
sections.explanation: The header comment sums up what the file is for: users, sessions, key ownership, and an audit trail. It uses `DatabaseSync` from `node:sqlite`, so no native npm dependency is needed. `mkdirSync` and `dirname` make sure the folder for the database file exists before the file is opened.

sections.title: Opening the DB and its schema
sections.explanation: `openDb` creates the parent directory, opens the database, and runs one `exec` that sets the pragmas and creates all tables idempotently with `IF NOT EXISTS`. WAL mode and a 5-second `busy_timeout` let reads and writes overlap without immediate `SQLITE_BUSY` errors, and `foreign_keys = ON` is needed for the `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `sessions` and `user_keys` to actually work. Sessions are keyed by `token_hash`, so raw session tokens are never stored. A `CHECK` constraint limits `role` to `admin` or `member` at the database level.

sections.title: Timestamps and audit log
sections.explanation: `now()` returns Unix seconds, which is the format every table uses. `audit` writes one row through a prepared statement with bound parameters, so the values cannot inject SQL. A missing user id becomes `NULL`, and `detail` is cut to 500 characters so a large payload cannot grow the audit table without limit.

sections.title: Public user projection
sections.explanation: `publicUser` is an allow-list projection: it copies only the fields that are safe to send to the browser and leaves out `password_hash`. It turns the SQLite integer `disabled` into a real boolean. The `u && {...}` guard means a missing row gives back a falsy value instead of throwing.

server/src/index.js.overview: Entry point of the Node.js dashboard backend (Express). It sets security headers and CSRF checks, mounts account routes, passes the public OpenAI-compatible gateway and the test-lab routes through to the Python Virodh engine, and implements the `/bff` (backend-for-frontend) API, where roles and per-user key ownership are enforced before engine admin endpoints are called. It also serves the built React SPA. This is the core of tour step 10.

sections.title: Topology, imports, configuration
sections.explanation: The ASCII diagram shows the two paths: browsers reach Node, which talks to the engine on port 8000, and API clients reach `/v1`, where the engine itself checks the API key. Paths, port, host, engine URL, and the users DB location come from environment variables with local defaults. `MEMBER_LIMITS` caps what non-admin users can create. `x-powered-by` is turned off and `trust proxy` is `false`, so the client-supplied `X-Forwarded-*` headers are not trusted.

sections.title: Security headers and CSRF guard
sections.explanation: A global middleware sets `nosniff`, `no-referrer`, and `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and applies a strict CSP everywhere except `/v1` and the engine's own API docs pages. For state-changing methods outside `/v1`, it rejects requests whose `Sec-Fetch-Site` is cross-site or whose `Origin` does not match the host. Together with SameSite=Lax cookies, this is the CSRF defence. `/v1` is left out because it uses bearer API keys, not cookies.

sections.title: Auth, pass-through, and test lab
sections.explanation: A JSON body parser limited to 200 kb is created once and attached only to the routes that need it. `/v1` is forwarded with `keepAuth: true`, so the client's `Authorization` header reaches the engine. A fixed list of health, docs, metrics, and sample paths is forwarded without auth. `/api` and `/static` need a signed-in user, and `/lab` redirects to sign-in when there is no session, so the original research dashboard is only available behind an account.

sections.title: BFF router helpers
sections.explanation: The `/bff` router requires a user on every route. The comment notes that the engine trusts Node, so roles must be enforced here. `send` passes the engine's status and body through, `ownKeyIds` looks up which keys belong to a user, and `playgroundLabel` builds the sanitised key name used for a user's playground runs. `wrap` turns any rejected promise, such as the engine being down, into a 502 response that includes only the error code.

sections.title: Models, policies, admin metrics
sections.explanation: Reading models and policies is allowed for any user, but saving or deleting a policy goes through `requireAdmin` and writes an audit entry when the engine returns 200. Policy names are passed through `encodeURIComponent` before they go into the engine path. The overview, usage, and system endpoints are admin-only, and `hours` is forced to a number with a default of 24 so no raw query string reaches the engine URL.

sections.title: API key management
sections.explanation: `GET /keys` adds owner information from the local `user_keys` table to the engine's key list. Members only see their own keys, and the internal `_uid` field is removed before the response is sent. `POST /keys` enforces the per-member active-key limit and caps `rpm` and `rpd`. It also sanitises the name, the policy, and the allowed-model list, then records ownership locally once the engine has created the key. `PATCH` returns 404 instead of 403 for keys a member does not own, so it does not reveal that the key exists, and only admins may change rate limits or allowed models.

sections.title: Request log and playground
sections.explanation: Only the known query filters are copied through. Members get extra `owner_key_ids` and `owner_key_name` filters, so they see only their own keys' traffic and their playground runs. The single-request route runs the same ownership check after fetching and returns 404 when it fails. The playground is streamed with `forward(... { console: true, user })`, which attaches the trusted console headers on the server side.

sections.title: User admin and audit view
sections.explanation: Admins can list users, with a count of keys for each, and change a user's role or disabled flag. The `PATCH` validates the role and refuses any change that would remove the last active admin. Disabling a user also deletes that user's sessions, so the change takes effect immediately. Every change is audited, and `/audit` returns the latest 100 entries joined with the user's email.

sections.title: Serving the React SPA
sections.explanation: If `web/dist` exists, static assets are served with a 1-hour cache, but HTML is served with `no-cache` so new deployments show up right away. A negative-lookahead regex sends every other path that is not an API path to `index.html`, so client-side routing works on a page refresh. If the app has not been built, a plain-text hint is served instead.

sections.title: Error handler and startup
sections.explanation: The last error middleware logs only the method, path, and message, and returns a generic JSON error, so stack traces never reach clients. It also maps body-parser 400s to `Malformed request.`. The server listens only when the file is run directly. Comparing `process.argv[1]` with the module path lets tests import `app` without opening a port.

server/src/proxy.js.overview: The bridge between the Node dashboard and the Python Virodh engine. `forward` streams a request and its response through unchanged (including SSE and multipart), after removing hop-by-hop and trust-carrying headers. `engineJson` makes buffered JSON calls to the engine's admin console API. As tour step 10 says, this means the dashboard never reimplements inspection; it only relays to the engine.

sections.title: Header filter lists
sections.explanation: `HOP` lists the hop-by-hop headers that must not be proxied, plus `host`, `cookie`, and `content-length`, which are handled on purpose elsewhere. Removing `cookie` means the dashboard session cookie never reaches the engine. `PRIVATE` lists the headers that carry console trust between Node and the engine. They are always removed from browser requests so a client cannot pretend to be the console.

sections.title: Engine config and console headers
sections.explanation: `engineFrom` parses the engine URL into host, port, and origin, and reads the optional `VIRODH_ADMIN_TOKEN` from the environment. `consoleHeaders` builds the trusted header set that only Node can add: the console flag, the admin token when one is set, and a sanitised, length-limited user email used for attribution.

sections.title: Streaming forward
sections.explanation: Client headers are copied without the HOP and PRIVATE headers, and `authorization` is removed too unless `keepAuth` is set, which is only the case for `/v1`. `Host` is rewritten to the engine's loopback address because the engine's console check expects it. The upstream response is piped back without `set-cookie`, so the engine cannot set cookies on the dashboard origin. A 200-second timeout, a 502 response on connection errors, and destroying the upstream request when the client disconnects all prevent hung or orphaned calls.

sections.title: Buffered JSON calls
sections.explanation: `engineJson` uses the global `fetch` with console headers, an optional JSON body, and a 60-second `AbortSignal.timeout`. A response body that is not JSON is tolerated and returned as `body: null`. The function returns `{status, body}` instead of throwing on HTTP errors, so the BFF routes can pass the engine's status through. Network failures still reject, and `wrap` in index.js turns them into a 502.

web/src/api.js.overview: The React app's same-origin data layer. It provides a `fetch` wrapper that normalises errors, an `AuthProvider` context that holds the signed-in user, and a `useLoad` hook for loading data. The session lives in an HttpOnly cookie, so the frontend never handles tokens. It talks to the Node backend from tour step 10 and is part of tour step 11.

sections.title: ApiError type
sections.explanation: The header comment states the security model: the session is an HttpOnly cookie and the app never sees the token. `ApiError` adds an HTTP `status` to a normal Error, so callers can tell apart cases such as unauthenticated (401), not found (404), and network failure (0).

sections.title: The api() fetch wrapper
sections.explanation: `api` sends cookies with `credentials: same-origin` and accepts either a JSON `body` or a `FormData` `form` (for image uploads). A network failure becomes `ApiError(0, ...)`. On HTTP errors it looks for a message in several error shapes (Node's `message`, OpenAI-style `error.message`, FastAPI's `detail`) and falls back to a generic one. A 401 from `/bff` dispatches a global `virodh:signed-out` event, so the whole app reacts to an expired session.

sections.title: AuthProvider context
sections.explanation: This is the React Context pattern mentioned in the tour's language lesson. `AuthProvider` loads `/auth/me` on mount, tracks `loading`, `user`, and `setupNeeded` (first-run admin setup), and clears the user when the signed-out event fires. `signIn`, `signUp`, and `signOut` update the shared state, and `signOut` ignores errors so the local sign-out always happens. It uses `createElement` instead of JSX because this is a plain `.js` file. `useAuth` gives any component access to the context.

sections.title: useLoad data hook
sections.explanation: `useLoad` runs an async loader whenever `deps` change and returns `[data, error, reload]`. Errors are stored in state instead of being thrown, so pages can render an `ErrorBox`. The eslint exception is on purpose: the caller controls the dependency list, which is how `Policies.jsx` reloads after a save.

web/src/main.jsx.overview: Entry point of the React single-page app. It loads fonts and global styles, defines a `Protected` route guard, declares the public pages and the nested authenticated `/app` routes (some admin-only), and mounts everything inside `StrictMode`, `BrowserRouter`, and `AuthProvider`. This is the starting point of tour step 11.

sections.title: Fonts, styles, page imports
sections.explanation: The Fontsource packages bundle web fonts locally, which works with the backend's `font-src 'self'` CSP because no font CDN is needed. Every page component is imported directly instead of lazy-loaded, which keeps the build simple for a dashboard of this size.

sections.title: Protected route guard
sections.explanation: `Protected` reads the auth context. It shows a loader while the session check is running, redirects anonymous users to `/signin` with a `next` parameter holding the current path, and sends non-admins who try an admin route back to `/app`. This guard only affects the UI. The real authorisation is done on the server by `requireUser` and `requireAdmin` in the Node backend.

sections.title: Route table
sections.explanation: The public routes are the landing page, sign-in, sign-up, and developer docs. `/app` renders `AppLayout` inside `Protected`, and its child routes appear in the layout's `<Outlet />`. Usage, Users, and System are also wrapped in `<Protected admin>`, which matches the Admin section of the sidebar. A catch-all route redirects unknown paths to `/`.

sections.title: Mounting the root
sections.explanation: `createRoot` mounts the app into `#root`. `AuthProvider` sits inside `BrowserRouter`, so auth state is available to every route, and `StrictMode` turns on React's extra development checks.

web/src/pages/app/Layout.jsx.overview: The authenticated dashboard shell. It provides a grouped sidebar (Build, Govern, Admin, Resources), a user card with sign-out, an engine-readiness indicator in the top bar, and an `<Outlet />` where the child pages render. It also exports `PageHead`, the shared page title component. This is the 'authenticated shell' described in tour step 11.

sections.title: Navigation model
sections.explanation: `NAV` describes the sidebar as data: each group has a title, a list of `[path, label, icon, end]` entries, and an optional admin-only flag. The `end` flag on Home makes `/app` highlighted only on the exact path and not on every child page. The Admin group carries the `true` flag, so members never see it.

sections.title: Shell state and readiness poll
sections.explanation: The mobile menu closes on every route change. An effect polls `/readyz` every 15 seconds to show whether the engine is up and which worker answered. The `alive` flag stops state updates after unmount, and the interval is cleared in the cleanup function. The user's initials for the avatar are built from their name.

sections.title: Sidebar rendering
sections.explanation: The groups are drawn from `NAV`, and admin-only groups are skipped for members. `NavLink` sets the `active` class through its `isActive` render callback. The Resources section links to the in-app docs, the engine's API reference, and the classic lab. The user card shows name, role, and email, and sign-out calls the context's `signOut` and then navigates to `/signin`.

sections.title: Main area and outlet
sections.explanation: The top bar has the mobile menu toggle, which sets `nav-open` on the root, and an engine status pill that reads Connecting, ready, or offline. `<Outlet />` renders whichever nested `/app/*` route matched in `main.jsx`.

sections.title: PageHead component
sections.explanation: `PageHead` gives every page the same header: a title, an optional subtitle, and a slot for actions on the right. It also updates `document.title` from the page title, so browser tabs and history show which dashboard page is open.

web/src/pages/app/Policies.jsx.overview: The dashboard's policy-profile editor. It lists the gateway policies from `/bff/policies`, and an `Editor` panel lets admins create, edit, or delete them. The fields map to the per-key policy model from tour step 9: mode, REVIEW action, block response, output guard, envelope, adversarial engine, blocked phrases, denied topics, and allowed models. Members see the same form in read-only mode. This is the policies page mentioned in tour step 11.

sections.title: Imports and blank template
sections.explanation: `BLANK` is the starting point for a new policy. Its defaults are conservative: `monitor` mode, so a new policy only logs until an operator turns on enforcement, REVIEW mapped to block, and the output guard and untrusted-image envelope both on. The field names match the backend's Pydantic policy model.

sections.title: Editor state, save, delete
sections.explanation: The editor keeps a local copy of the policy and resets it whenever another policy is selected. Blocked phrases are edited as text with one phrase per line. `save` checks that there is a name, removes the server-only fields (`name`, `updated`, `keys_using`) from the body, splits and trims the phrases, drops empty topic rows, and sends a `PUT` to `/bff/policies/:name`, which the Node backend allows only for admins. `del` asks for confirmation first, and afterwards the page goes back to the `default` policy. `setTopic` updates one topic row without mutating the array.

sections.title: Core policy switches
sections.explanation: The whole form sits in a `fieldset disabled={ro}`, so a single attribute makes every input read-only for members. The name can only be set when the policy is new, because it is the policy's key. `Seg` segmented controls choose enforce or monitor, what to do on REVIEW, whether blocked requests get a refusal or an API error, and the adversarial-engine mode. In that last control the option labelled 'Hold' has the value `enforce`. Two switches turn the output guard and the untrusted-image envelope on or off.

sections.title: Phrases, topics, allowed models
sections.explanation: The help text says blocked phrases are matched as whole words, case-insensitively, including in text found inside images. Operator rules (denied topics) are editable rows of name, description, and block or review action. The UI notes that these rules are checked by the policy classifier and that the request is held if the check is unavailable, which is the fail-safe described in tour step 9. The allowed-models list is built from switches, and an empty list means all models are allowed.

sections.title: Errors and action buttons
sections.explanation: An `ErrorBox` shows any error from saving or deleting. The action buttons appear only for admins, the save button shows a spinner while `busy`, and Delete is hidden for new policies and for the built-in `default` policy, which cannot be deleted.

sections.title: Policies page and selection
sections.explanation: The page loads the policies and the model list with `useLoad`. `sel` holds the selected policy name, and an empty string means a new policy based on `BLANK`. If the selected name is not found, the first policy is used. The left column shows clickable cards with each policy's mode, rule count, and number of keys using it. After a save, `onSaved` selects the saved policy and calls `reload()`, so the list and the editor stay in sync with the backend.

web/src/ui.jsx.overview: The dashboard's shared component and helper library: number and time formatters, labels for gateway actions, layout pieces (Panel, Stat, Table), form controls (Seg, Switch), toasts and clipboard copy, code tabs, a modal drawer, small SVG charts, and the icon set. The header comment states a security rule: server data is always rendered as escaped React text, with no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Tour step 11 introduces it as the shared UI library.

sections.title: Formatters and action labels
sections.explanation: The helpers format numbers, milliseconds, percentages, Unix-second timestamps (time only for today, otherwise date and time), and relative 'ago' text. Each one returns `—` for missing values so tables never show `undefined`. `ACTION` maps the gateway's internal action codes, such as `monitor_forwarded` and `withheld`, to readable labels, and unknown codes are shown as they are.

sections.title: Logo, Chip, loading, errors
sections.explanation: `Logo` is an inline SVG, so no image request is needed. `Chip` maps the guard decisions ALLOW, REVIEW, and BLOCK to the matching CSS colour classes, and an explicit `kind` can override that. `Spinner`, `Loading`, and `ErrorBox` are the shared feedback components, and `ErrorBox` renders nothing when there is no error.

sections.title: Panel, Stat, Table, controls
sections.explanation: `Panel` is a titled section with optional actions and a subtitle. `Table` is driven by column definitions (`{label, get, num, wrap}`), shows an empty state when there are no rows, and makes rows clickable when `onRow` is passed. `Seg` is a segmented control made of buttons that use `aria-pressed` for accessibility. `Switch` wraps a checkbox and passes a boolean to `onChange`.

sections.title: Toast and clipboard
sections.explanation: `toast` works outside React: it creates or reuses a single `.toast` element with `role=status`, sets `textContent` (never HTML), and removes the element after 2.6 seconds, resetting the timer for each new message. `copyText` uses the async Clipboard API and shows a toast with manual-copy instructions if copying fails.

sections.title: Code tabs and Drawer
sections.explanation: `Code` shows tabbed code snippets, such as SDK examples, with a copy button for the active tab. `Drawer` is a modal side panel with `role=dialog` and `aria-modal`. It closes when Escape is pressed or the overlay is clicked, and the keydown listener is removed again in the effect cleanup.

sections.title: Decision series and simple charts
sections.explanation: `DECISIONS` defines the chart series with CSS-variable colours, so charts follow the theme. `Legend` can show totals for each series. `SegBar` is a single stacked bar with an `aria-label` that lists the counts, and `HBars` draws horizontal bars scaled to the largest value. The comment states the rule that status colours always come with a legend and labels, so colour is never the only way information is shown.

sections.title: StackedColumns SVG chart
sections.explanation: This is a hand-written stacked column chart, so no chart library is needed. `niceMax` rounds the y-axis maximum to a 1/2/5 multiple, `tick` shortens labels to K format, and `topRounded` builds an SVG path that rounds only the top of the uppermost segment. Each bucket has a transparent, focusable hit rectangle that sets `hover` on mouse and keyboard focus. The tooltip's position is clamped to the container width.

sections.title: Icon set
sections.explanation: `Icon` is an object of pre-built inline SVG elements that use `currentColor`, so they take on the surrounding text colour. `Layout.jsx` uses them in the sidebar. Inline SVG fits the strict `img-src` CSP and needs no extra requests.

config/adversarial_calibration.json.overview: Calibration data for the adversarial-image engine (tour step 12). It stores clean-image percentiles for each rule-based feature, the chosen decision threshold with the sweep behind it, the calibration-domain gate, and the settings of the learned fusion model (path, threshold, and clean medians and IQRs for explaining deviations). `engine.py` and `detectors.py` read this file so features are normalised the same way in evaluation and in production.

sections.title: Fit metadata
sections.explanation: This records where the calibration came from: fitted on the validation split, using 50 clean images for the percentiles and 200 benign and 200 adversarial samples for the threshold sweep. Keeping this next to the numbers shows how much data the thresholds rest on.

sections.title: Clean-image feature percentiles
sections.explanation: Each feature has its p0.5, p5, p95, and p99.5 on clean images. `_score` in `detectors.py` maps a measurement to risk 0 at or below p95 and risk 1 at or above p99.5. For features where a low value is suspicious (`residual_kurtosis`, `channel_corr`) it uses the lower tail, p5 to p0.5. `squeeze_flip_frac` has p95 equal to p99.5 (0.8), so it falls back to the step function in `_score`.

sections.title: Chosen thresholds and rule
sections.explanation: The operating threshold is 0.81. At that value the sweep shows 8.5% of adversarial samples flagged and a 5% benign flag rate. The `rule` explains the choice: the highest adversarial flag rate with a benign rate of at most 5%, taken from the middle of a stable plateau (0.78 to 0.83). A second `sensitive_threshold` (0.66) uses a benign set that leaves out the Gaussian-noise control. Both values are written down openly instead of only the better-looking one.

sections.title: Threshold sweep table
sections.explanation: This is the full sweep from 0.05 to 0.99, with the adversarial and benign flag rates at each step. It is kept as data so the calibration can be audited or plotted. It also shows the trade-off honestly: low thresholds flag many benign images, and at the 5% benign limit the rule-based detectors catch only a small share of attacks.

sections.title: Calibration domain gate
sections.explanation: `flat_ratio_max` is 0.6. Images with more perfectly flat pixels than that (documents, screenshots, graphics) are outside the natural-photo domain the detectors were calibrated on. `engine.py` reports them as not analysed instead of scoring them, which avoids false positives caused by sharp text edges.

sections.title: Learned fusion model config
sections.explanation: This section points to the active HistGradientBoosting model (`iter4_noise_robust`), trained on the train split with noise augmentation, and its threshold of 0.7139 chosen on validation. `features` fixes the order of the 25-dimensional vector built in `learned.py`. `clean_medians` and `clean_iqr` let the engine explain a positive result as a number of IQRs away from clean images.

sections.title: Previous iteration (iter3)
sections.explanation: An earlier model's settings (threshold 0.5278, same feature set and clean statistics) are kept under `learned_iter3`. The engine reads only the `learned` key, so this block is a record for comparison and possible rollback, not an active configuration.

guard/adversarial/classifier.py.overview: Local image-classifier adapter for the adversarial engine: a torchvision ResNet18 with ImageNet weights, loaded once as a thread-safe singleton. It defines the shared pixel space (a 224x224 crop in [0,1], with normalisation inside the model) and two access views: `WhiteBox` (probabilities, and gradients through the classifier) and `BlackBox` (top-k labels only, with a query budget). The detectors from tour step 12 use these views to measure how the classifier's predictions react to small changes.

sections.title: Module doc and preprocessing
sections.explanation: The docstring explains the main design choice: all analysis works on the 224x224 model-input crop in [0,1]. `_PREPROCESS` resizes to 256 and centre-crops to 224 but leaves out ImageNet normalisation, so pixel-level measurements and gradients refer to real pixel values. The mean and std constants are the standard ImageNet statistics.

sections.title: Normalising wrapper and Prediction
sections.explanation: `_Normalized` puts the mean and std subtraction inside the network as registered buffers, so they move with `.to(device)` and are part of the computation. `Prediction` is a small dataclass with the top label, its index, its confidence, and the top-k list.

sections.title: ResNet18Classifier
sections.explanation: The constructor picks CUDA when available and CPU otherwise, loads the ImageNet categories, and freezes all parameters. `to_tensor` and `to_image` convert between PIL images and tensors in the shared pixel space. `logits` and `predict` run under `torch.inference_mode()` for fast inference without gradients. `loss_grad` deliberately runs outside inference mode and returns the input gradient. The docstring says gradient access is used to generate controlled test perturbations in evaluation.

sections.title: WhiteBox access view
sections.explanation: `WhiteBox` exposes full softmax probabilities and argmax labels, with `mode = white_box`. The consistency detector checks `access.mode` to decide whether it can compare full probability vectors (an L1 distance) or only labels.

sections.title: BlackBox access view
sections.explanation: `BlackBox` models a weaker access level. Each query is counted against a budget and raises `QueryBudgetExceeded` once the budget is used up. `probs` is refused unless `with_probs` is set, and even then every entry except the top-k is set to zero. `loss_grad` always raises. These limits are enforced in code, so black-box results really do reflect the reduced information.

sections.title: Thread-safe singleton
sections.explanation: `get_classifier` builds the ResNet18 once and returns it from then on. A `threading.Lock` stops concurrent first requests from loading the weights twice. Loading the model is the expensive part, so the engine and the evaluation scripts all share this one instance.

guard/adversarial/detectors.py.overview: The four rule-based adversarial-image detectors from tour step 12: statistical (residual noise statistics), frequency (share of high-frequency spectral energy), consistency (prediction stability under small benign transformations, following Feature Squeezing), and local_region (grid cells with outlying noise). Each one turns raw measurements into a risk in [0,1], based on how far the value lies beyond the clean-image percentiles in the calibration file, and returns a `DetectorResult` with readable evidence. The docstring makes the point that unusual statistics are evidence of suspiciousness, not proof of an attack.

sections.title: Module doc and imports
sections.explanation: The docstring summarises each detector and credits Feature Squeezing (Xu et al., NDSS 2018) for the consistency idea. The detectors depend on `guard.adversarial.features` for the low-level measurements and on the shared `DetectorResult` schema, so their output fits into the same reporting format as the text-guard detectors.

sections.title: Quantile scoring and result builder
sections.explanation: `_score` maps a value linearly from p95 (risk 0) to p99.5 (risk 1) of the clean distribution. For features where a low value is suspicious, it negates the value and uses the lower tail. When the two quantiles are equal it falls back to a step function, and without calibration it returns 0, so an uncalibrated detector never raises an alarm on its own. `_result` builds the `DetectorResult`, setting suspicious at 0.5, rounding the numbers, and recording the run time.

sections.title: Statistical detector
sections.explanation: This detector measures the residual noise in flat image regions (`smooth_noise`), the kurtosis of the residual, and how strongly the residual is correlated across colour channels. Unusually low kurtosis or correlation counts as suspicious. Risk is `0.7 * max + 0.3 * mean` of the three scores, so one strong signal counts most and agreement between signals adds a little. Evidence text is produced only for features that scored above zero, and confidence is lower when there is no calibration.

sections.title: Frequency detector
sections.explanation: This detector computes the share of spectral energy at high frequencies on the grayscale image and scores it against the clean-image percentiles. Its confidence is lower than the statistical detector's because high-frequency energy also comes from ordinary texture.

sections.title: Benign squeeze transforms
sections.explanation: `_squeezes` creates five small, harmless versions of the input: 5-bit colour depth, a 3x3 median blur, a JPEG round-trip at quality 75, a downscale to 87.5% and back up, and a 4% brightness increase. A natural image should be classified about the same under all of them. The JPEG version is re-encoded in memory with PIL.

sections.title: Consistency detector
sections.explanation: The original image and its five variants are classified together in one batch. In white-box mode the largest L1 shift in the probability vector is scored, and any transform that changes the predicted class is listed. In black-box mode only the fraction of label flips is available, so confidence is fixed at 0.3 and the evidence says that uncertainty is higher. The details include the query budget used, which shows the cost of the weaker access level.

sections.title: Local-region detector
sections.explanation: The residual map is split into a 4x4 grid. The noise level in each cell is compared with the others using a robust z-score (median and MAD scaled by 1.4826). Cells with z of 3.5 or more are reported as regions. When `crop_box` is given, their boxes are converted from 224px model coordinates back to the uploaded image. The details note that this finds localised anomalies and is not a complete patch detector.

guard/adversarial/engine.py.overview: The orchestrator of the adversarial-image engine from tour step 12. It runs the ResNet18 prediction and the four detectors, combines their risks without double-counting correlated pixel signals, optionally replaces that score with the learned fusion model, and returns an `AdversarialReport`. It also applies a calibration-domain gate, so documents and graphics are reported as not analysed instead of being scored, and it keeps the notes about what the engine can and cannot claim honest.

sections.title: Design doc and constants
sections.explanation: The docstring gives the fusion formula. Pixel risk is the maximum of statistical, frequency, and 0.7 times local_region, because all three measure the same pixel noise. Behaviour risk is the consistency score. The two are combined noisy-OR style, each weighted 0.9. The docstring also keeps three statements apart: suspicious characteristics, whether the classifier changed (known only in controlled simulations), and the attack family (never inferred). The calibration path and the default domain gate (0.6) are constants.

sections.title: Report type and calibration loading
sections.explanation: `AdversarialReport` holds the risk, the suspicious flag, the threshold, whether the engine is calibrated, the access mode, the prediction, each detector's result, the flagged regions, timings, notes, and the domain fields `applicable` and `flat_ratio`. `to_dict` adds `engine: adversarial` for API output. `load_calibration` returns `None` when the file is missing or malformed, so the engine can still run in uncalibrated mode.

sections.title: Crop mapping and rule-based fusion
sections.explanation: `crop_box_for` reproduces the scale and offset of Resize(256) followed by CenterCrop(224), so the local_region detector can map grid boxes back to the original image. `fuse` uses only detectors whose status is `ok`. A failed detector counts as 0, so it does not distort the score, and the failure is still reported separately.

sections.title: Engine init and learned fusion
sections.explanation: The constructor gets the shared classifier, loads the calibration, and loads the joblib model only if the calibration's `learned` entry points to a file that exists. `joblib` is imported lazily. `_learned` extracts the shared feature vector (`learned.py`), predicts the probability of an adversarial image, and, when that probability is above the threshold, explains it with the three features that deviate most from clean images, measured in IQR units.

sections.title: Calibration-domain gate
sections.explanation: Before any detector runs, `scan_tensor` measures the share of perfectly flat pixels. If it is above the gate, the image is treated as a document, screenshot, or graphic and returned with `applicable=False`, risk 0, and every detector marked `skipped`, along with a note explaining why. This prevents false positives on images the detectors were never calibrated for, while still reporting the classifier's prediction.

sections.title: Detector run, fusion, and notes
sections.explanation: The access mode chooses between a WhiteBox view and a budgeted BlackBox view. The four detectors run one after another, each inside a try/except that records `status=error` instead of dropping the result. When a learned model is loaded, its probability and threshold replace the rule-based score. A failure in that model is recorded too, and the rule-based score is kept. The notes always include the scope disclaimer, plus warnings for uncalibrated mode and for low clean-prediction confidence, where the consistency signal is less reliable. `suspicious` is true only when there is a threshold and the risk reaches it.

sections.title: Entry points and singletons
sections.explanation: `scan_image` and `scan_bytes` convert PIL images or raw bytes into the model tensor and pass the crop box along. `get_engine` lazily creates one shared engine, and `reload_engine` replaces it so that a new calibration or model can be picked up without restarting the process.

guard/adversarial/learned.py.overview: Builds the fixed-order feature vector the adversarial image engine scores with. Evaluation and the live API both call it, so a model trained offline sees exactly the same features in production. It mixes cheap pixel statistics (noise residuals, spectrum, channel correlation, region outliers) with signals about how the classifier behaves on the image and on five 'squeezed' copies of it. This is the 'learned.py' feature vector described in tour step 12.

sections.title: Feature catalogue
sections.explanation: The docstring splits the features into a *pixel* group and a *behaviour* group, and `FEATURE_NAMES` fixes their order. That order matters: `vector()` serialises the dict in this order, so any trained model or calibration percentiles depend on it. To add a feature you have to append its name here and also emit it in `extract`, or `vector` will raise a `KeyError`.

sections.title: Feature-squeezing transforms
sections.explanation: `_squeezes` returns five 'squeezed' versions of the input tensor: 5-bit colour quantisation, a 3x3 median blur, a JPEG quality-75 round trip, downscale-then-upscale to 87.5%, and a 4% brightness lift. Each one tends to destroy small adversarial perturbations while leaving natural image content mostly intact. A big change in the classifier's prediction under squeezing is therefore a classic sign of adversarial input. The conversion between PIL/OpenCV uint8 arrays and NCHW float tensors happens inline.

sections.title: Region outlier score
sections.explanation: The residual magnitude is split into a 4x4 grid and the standard deviation of each cell is computed. The function then returns the largest robust z-score, using the median and the MAD scaled by 1.4826 so it is comparable to a standard deviation. This flags *localised* perturbations, such as an adversarial patch, that a global statistic would average away. The `1e-6` term guards against division by zero on perfectly flat images.

sections.title: Pixel statistics
sections.explanation: `extract` first computes a high-pass residual and restricts it to smooth regions (`smooth_mask`), where real images have little fine noise and perturbations stand out. It histograms the non-zero 8-bit residual values to get the concentration (`res_top2_mass`) and entropy. Sparse residuals fall back to neutral values. The same noise measure is repeated at half resolution, and the ratio `noise_ratio_scales` separates scale-invariant camera noise from pixel-level perturbations. Spectrum, kurtosis, channel-correlation and flat-ratio helpers come from `guard.adversarial.features`.

sections.title: Classifier behaviour features
sections.explanation: The original image and its five squeezes go through the classifier in one batched forward pass. From that it derives confidence, entropy, the top-2 margin, the L1 change in the probability vector for each squeeze, the drop in confidence on the top class, and the fraction of squeezes that flip the top label. A separate backward pass computes the size of the input gradient of the top class's log-probability (`log_gnorm`). Adversarial examples often sit in regions where the gradient is unusually saturated or unusually small. This uses `torch.autograd.grad`, so it does not touch any `.grad` state on the model parameters.

sections.title: Ordered vector export
sections.explanation: `vector` turns the feature dict into a float64 numpy array in `FEATURE_NAMES` order. This is what the learned fusion model and the clean-image calibration percentiles consume. Keeping the conversion in one place stops the train and serve code paths from drifting apart.

app/main.py.overview: Entry point for the original research FastAPI app (separate from the later Virodh gateway). It installs a small security middleware, maps errors to uniform JSON responses, mounts the scan, system, evaluate and adversarial routers under /api, and serves the static dashboard. Tour step 13 introduces it as the pre-Virodh way of exposing Threat Guard.

sections.title: Bootstrap and imports
sections.explanation: The repository root goes onto `sys.path` so the app runs from any working directory. `tg_bootstrap` is imported only for its side effects: it loads `.env` secrets and patches the upstream config loader before anything else imports upstream code. `MAX_BODY` caps request size at 11 MB. `TG_API_TOKEN` optionally turns on bearer-token auth for `/api/*`.

sections.title: App and request middleware
sections.explanation: The HTTP middleware rejects oversized `/api/` requests early, using the `Content-Length` header, so they are refused before the body is parsed. It also enforces the optional bearer token. Every response gets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. One caveat: the size check trusts the declared header, so a chunked request without `Content-Length` skips it.

sections.title: Uniform error handlers
sections.explanation: Three exception handlers give every error the same `{error, message}` JSON shape. Validation errors return a generic message rather than echoing field details. The catch-all handler logs the full traceback on the server but tells the client only that the request was not forwarded, so internals never leak to callers.

sections.title: Routers and dashboard
sections.explanation: Each feature area lives in its own `APIRouter` module under `app/routes`, and all of them mount under the `/api` prefix with OpenAPI tags. The `dashboard/` folder is served at `/static`, and `/` returns its `index.html` (excluded from the API schema). This is the same `include_router` composition pattern the Virodh server uses later.

app/services.py.overview: Shared services behind the research API routes: a lazily built ThreatGuard singleton, cached target-model adapters from the upstream OmniSafeBench-MM registry, a sliding-window rate limiter, in-process session statistics, and an opt-in JSONL history of live responses. Tour step 13 describes it as the backing layer for app/main.py.

sections.title: Imports and target catalogue
sections.explanation: `tg_bootstrap` must be imported before any upstream module (`config.config_loader`, `core.*`), and the `# isort: split` marker stops import sorting from moving it. `TARGETS` maps model names from `config/model_config.yaml` to dashboard labels, so changing the VLM means editing config, not code. `DEFAULT_TARGET` picks the free-tier Gemini model.

sections.title: Lazy guard and model cache
sections.explanation: `guard()` builds one `ThreatGuard` under a lock the first time it is called, so importing the module stays cheap and concurrent requests share a single engine. `_model` validates the name against `TARGETS` (an allow-list) and creates adapters through `UNIFIED_REGISTRY` once per name. Both caches share the same `_lock`.

sections.title: Calling the target VLM
sections.explanation: `ask_model` writes the image to a temporary PNG because the upstream adapters expect a file path, and the `finally` block always deletes it. When `guarded` is true the prompt is wrapped with the trust-separating envelope before it is sent. `adversarial_scan` imports the adversarial engine inside the function, so torch is loaded only when that route is actually used.

sections.title: Sliding-window rate limiter
sections.explanation: `RateLimiter` keeps a deque of monotonic timestamps per client key, drops entries older than the window, and refuses the request once the count reaches the limit. It is exact rather than bucketed, and thread-safe through its own lock. The scan limiter defaults to 20 requests per minute and can be changed with `TG_SCAN_RATE_PER_MIN`. The state lives in process memory, so it is per-process only.

sections.title: Session statistics
sections.explanation: `SessionStats` counts decisions, normalised attack categories (it strips suffixes after ` | `, `:` and ` (`), fail-safe events, forwards and output-guard withholds. It also keeps the last 500 latencies. `snapshot` computes the mean and a nearest-rank p95 using ceiling arithmetic (`-(-95*n//100)`). The note it returns is a deliberate honesty marker: unlabelled live traffic cannot measure false positives.

sections.title: Opt-in response history
sections.explanation: `save_history` writes nothing unless `demo.save_live_responses` is enabled in `config/guard.yaml`. When it is, each guarded/unguarded comparison is appended as one JSON line to `logs/live_responses.jsonl`, keeping only the top three reasons and summary fields for the unguarded run. Writes are serialised with `_hist_lock`. `read_history` returns the most recent N rows, newest first. The late imports are marked `noqa: E402` because this block was added below the main services.

config/plugins.yaml.overview: Plugin registry in the upstream OmniSafeBench-MM format. It maps each attack, model, defense and evaluator name to a [module path, class name] pair that the unified registry imports at runtime. Comments label each entry as UPSTREAM (copied unmodified) or OURS (tg_plugins), which is how tour step 13 shows Threat Guard plugging into the benchmark toolbox.

sections.title: Format header
sections.explanation: The file declares its schema version and explains the `name -> [python_module_path, class_name]` convention. Because classes are resolved by dotted path, you add a plugin by adding one line here, with no code change in the registry.

sections.title: Attack plugins
sections.explanation: Published attacks (FigStep and the MML variants) point to upstream code. Several names, such as `mml_wr`, `mml_base64` and `mml_mirror`, reuse the same class, and the variant is chosen by per-attack config. The project's own synthetic attacks (QR code, three canary techniques and a benign passthrough) live in `tg_plugins`. All three canary entries share `CanaryAttack` and differ only in config. HADES is commented out because it needs heavy dependencies.

sections.title: Model adapters
sections.explanation: Provider names map to `CompactVLMModel`, which adds image downscaling and fail-loud image loading to the upstream OpenAI model. The `*_app` variants map to `AppVLMModel`, which also simulates an app-side QR scanner that appends decoded QR text to the prompt. That is what makes QR-borne attacks meaningful. Generic `openai` and `any` fall back to the upstream class.

sections.title: Defenses and evaluators
sections.explanation: The upstream AdaShield defense is kept as a baseline next to `threat_guard`, the project's own defense plugin, so both can be benchmarked through the same pipeline. Judging uses the upstream `default_judge`, which keeps attack-success scoring independent of the guard under test.

tg_plugins/attacks/canary.py.overview: Synthetic, harmless-by-design 'canary' hijack attack for the benchmark. Each generated image carries a text instruction that tries to make the model reply with a unique code word, so attack success can be measured exactly by checking whether that token appears in the reply. It supports three delivery techniques (printed sign, faint text on a fictional resume, QR code) and two template pools that keep a held-out test wording. Tour step 13 introduces it as the canary attack plugin.

sections.title: Purpose and techniques
sections.explanation: The docstring sets the ground rules: nothing harmful is ever requested, and success is an exact string check. The three techniques model different hiding places: visible typography, near-invisible grey text in a document-screening scenario, and a QR code that only an app-side scanner would decode. Image helpers such as wrapped text, fonts, seeded RNG and QR posters come from `tg_plugins.common`.

sections.title: Template pools A and B
sections.explanation: `TEMPLATE_POOLS` contains override-style instruction templates with a `{token}` placeholder, split into a *photo* family and a *resume* family. Pool A may be used while developing and calibrating the guard. Pool B uses deliberately different wording and is held out for the test split, which keeps the reported detection numbers honest against overfitting to known phrasings. The benign user prompts (`PHOTO_PROMPTS`, `RESUME_PROMPT`) give the injected instruction a legitimate task to try to override.

sections.title: Fictional resume data and config
sections.explanation: Name, skill and project lists fill in fictional resumes. `canary_token` builds a per-case code word from the case ID, so every reply can be attributed to its own test case. `CanaryConfig` selects the technique, the grey level of the hidden line (222 on white is barely visible, 255 would be invisible), and which template pool to draw from.

sections.title: Image builders
sections.explanation: `_typo` extends the seed photo with a pale-yellow band and prints the instruction on it in bold, like a sign. `_resume` draws a realistic-looking resume (name, CGPA, skills, projects, experience, achievements) from the seeded RNG and then writes the instruction near the bottom in the configured faint grey. That is the low-contrast signal the obfuscation detector and contrast-boost OCR pass are built to recover. `draw_wrapped` returns the next y position, which lays out the sections in sequence.

sections.title: Test case generation
sections.explanation: `generate_test_case` seeds the RNG from (`canary`, technique, case ID), so regenerating the dataset gives identical images. It picks a template from the configured pool, renders the image for the chosen technique, saves it, and returns an upstream `TestCase`. The metadata records the canary token, a template ID prefixed by the pool letter, and the injected text. The evaluation later passes these to `output_guard.complied` to tell real obedience apart from a reply that merely quotes the instruction.

tg_plugins/defenses/threat_guard.py.overview: Adapter that exposes Threat Guard as an upstream OmniSafeBench-MM BaseDefense. ALLOW decisions are forwarded with the trust-separation envelope. REVIEW and BLOCK go through the upstream block_input() path, so the target model is never called. The guard's decision and evidence are copied into test-case metadata so they reach the benchmark's response files. Tour step 13 notes that this plugin forwards only ALLOW decisions.

sections.title: Lazy guard singleton
sections.explanation: The docstring states the defense contract. `get_guard` builds one `ThreatGuard` under a lock the first time it is used, the same pattern as `app/services.py`. Benchmark workers therefore share one engine and avoid reloading OCR and config for every case.

sections.title: Compact report metadata
sections.explanation: `compact` flattens a `ScanReport` into `tg_`-prefixed fields: decision, risk, category, fail-safe flag, the top six reasons, per-detector risk and status, latency, and up to 300 characters of each extracted segment. `segments[0]` is the user prompt and is skipped. The prefix keeps guard fields easy to tell apart from upstream metadata.

sections.title: Reusing recorded scans
sections.explanation: `recorded_scan` lazily indexes every `output/*/guard_scans/*.jsonl` file by (attack, test_case_id). Benchmark runs then reuse exactly the decisions measured by `eval/scan_cases.py` instead of re-scanning, which keeps the reported metrics and the guarded replies consistent. Fail-safe rows are deliberately not indexed, so those cases are scanned again live.

sections.title: apply_defense decision path
sections.explanation: The method takes the recorded decision if one exists and otherwise runs a live scan, tagging `tg_source` either way. Only `Decision.ALLOW` produces a defended case with the prompt wrapped by `wrap_prompt` and the original image. Anything else calls `block_input` with a short refusal that names the first reason. The target model is never called for blocked cases, which is the fail-closed behaviour the evaluation counts on.

eval/calibrate.py.overview: Chooses the REVIEW and BLOCK risk thresholds using only the validation split, and writes eval/reports/calibration.json together with the full sweep. It uses a documented Youden-style rule (J = attack flag rate minus benign flag rate) with false-positive caps, and picks the middle of the near-optimal plateau to avoid overfitting. Tour step 14 calls it the validation-only threshold picker.

sections.title: Documented selection rule
sections.explanation: The docstring states the rule before any code runs, so the thresholds can be audited. Fail-safe rows are excluded because they do not depend on the threshold. The benign flag rate is capped at 5% for REVIEW and 2% for BLOCK (`FPR_REVIEW_MAX`, `FPR_BLOCK_MAX`), and BLOCK must sit at least 0.2 above REVIEW so an uncertain band remains. `eval/` goes onto `sys.path` so the sibling `common` module can be imported.

sections.title: Loading and sweeping
sections.explanation: Attack rows come from the `val` scans and benign rows from `benign_val`, and fail-safe rows are filtered out. The script exits early with a hint if the scans have not been produced yet. For every threshold from 0.05 to 0.99 it records the share of attacks and of benign cases with risk at or above the threshold, plus J.

sections.title: Plateau-middle selection
sections.explanation: `plateau_mid` finds every candidate whose J is within 0.01 of the best and returns the middle one, not the lowest edge. On a small validation set the edge is the most overfitted choice, and the middle is more robust. BLOCK is chosen with the same rule on a stricter candidate set. If no candidate meets the constraints, `or [review]` falls back to the REVIEW point so the script still produces output.

sections.title: Report and console output
sections.explanation: The output JSON records sample sizes, excluded fail-safe counts, the rule in plain words, the suggested thresholds, both plateau ranges and the full sweep, so reviewers can check the choice. The console shows every fifth sweep row. The script does not edit `config/guard.yaml` itself: applying the thresholds is an explicit manual step.

eval/metrics.py.overview: Builds the final evaluation summary on the test split and writes eval/reports/summary.json, which /api/metrics serves. It combines guard scan decisions, unguarded and guarded model replies, and upstream judge verdicts into per-attack and benign tables. Every attack-success number is labelled with how it was measured. Tour step 14 describes it as the test-split metrics combiner.

sections.title: Sources and success definitions
sections.explanation: The docstring lists each data source and how attack success is defined. Canary attacks use an exact check (did the reply obey the hidden instruction). Harmful attacks use the upstream LLM judge, falling back to a clearly labelled non-refusal proxy. Shared helpers such as `scans`, `responses`, `decision` and `pct` come from `eval/common.py`. `TARGET` fixes the target model the report is about.

sections.title: Judge results and attack success
sections.explanation: `judge_results` reads the upstream evaluation JSONL files for one defense into a map from (attack, case) to success. `attack_success` returns (successes, n, method). For canary attacks it calls `output_guard.complied` with the token and the injected text, so a reply that only quotes the instruction does not count. For harmful attacks it uses judge verdicts only when every row has one, and otherwise falls back to the refusal-regex proxy.

sections.title: Per-attack table
sections.explanation: Decisions are recomputed from the stored risk using the current `config/guard.yaml` thresholds. Detection rates count only fully inspected cases, and fail-safe holds are reported in a separate column. The guarded success rate is *measured* on the same case IDs as the unguarded column when a guarded run exists, with blocked cases counted as failed attacks. Otherwise it is *estimated* as attacks the guard allowed that succeeded without it, and labelled as an estimate.

sections.title: Benign false positives
sections.explanation: Benign cases are split into easy and hard negatives (images with text, QR codes, the word 'ignore', mirroring, and so on) using `_hard_ids`. False-positive rates are computed over inspected cases only. Benign task success with the guard is measured where guarded rows exist (rows that are still missing are excluded, not counted as failures) and estimated otherwise.

sections.title: Summary assembly and output
sections.explanation: The summary has headline numbers, three tables (per-attack, benign, latency with median and p95) and explicit methodology notes: thresholds were tuned on validation only, canary test cases use the held-out pool B, samples are small, and HADES has not been evaluated. Both the dashboard and the console printout read this single JSON, so the numbers and their caveats always travel together.

sections.title: Hard-negative ID cache
sections.explanation: `_hard_ids` loads the benign behaviour files for the test and validation splits once and caches the IDs whose `benign_type` starts with `hard`. A module-level global serves as a simple memo, which is enough for a one-shot script.

eval/virodh_e2e.py.overview: End-to-end check of a running Virodh gateway through the official OpenAI Python SDK and the real guard engine. It creates temporary API keys through the loopback admin console, runs a numbered series of PASS/FAIL checks, revokes the keys and writes eval/reports/virodh_e2e.json. Tour step 14 describes it as exercising the gateway through the OpenAI SDK.

sections.title: Setup and image helpers
sections.explanation: The docstring warns that hosted classifiers are really called (quota is used), but the target model is called only for requests the gateway forwards. `ADMIN` is the console header the admin API requires. `data_url` builds inline base64 image URLs, and `text_png` draws lines of text onto a white PNG, falling back to the default font when Arial is missing.

sections.title: Synthetic operator-rule fixtures
sections.explanation: `EXAM` mimics an exam paper and `TEXTBOOK` mimics a textbook paragraph on the same physics topic. Together they form a matched positive/negative pair for the opt-in `exam-integrity` operator policy: the exam image should be blocked and the explanatory textbook page should be allowed.

sections.title: Run harness
sections.explanation: `Run` wraps an `httpx.Client` for admin calls. `key()` creates a key with a chosen policy and rate limit and remembers its ID, `check()` records and prints one result, and `cleanup()` revokes every key created during the run so no live credentials are left behind.

sections.title: Core SDK checks
sections.explanation: The checks cover readiness, `models.list`, a benign text completion, the demo attack and benign samples sent as multimodal messages, cache behaviour on a repeated request, and SSE streaming. Gateway metadata is read from the non-standard `virodh` field through `model_extra`. Headers like `x-virodh-cache` are read with `with_raw_response`. An attack passes if its action is `blocked` or `withheld`, and a benign sample passes if it is `forwarded`.

sections.title: Scan API, policy and rate limits
sections.explanation: The `/v1/guard/scan` endpoint must flag an attack sample and return text found in the image as evidence, without any model call. A key on the strict policy must make the SDK raise `BadRequestError` with code `content_filter` for a clearly harmful text request, which shows the error-style block response. A key limited to 2 requests per minute must get a `RateLimitError` (429) on the third call. `max_retries=0` stops the SDK from hiding these errors by retrying.

sections.title: Operator rule and report
sections.explanation: Unless `--skip-exam` is set, the exam-integrity key must block the exam image and forward the textbook image, and the default key must still forward the exam image, which shows the rule is opt-in. Afterwards keys are revoked, a JSON report is written, and the process exits non-zero if any check failed, so the script can gate CI.

tests/test_guard.py.overview: Pytest unit tests for the Threat Guard engine with the hosted classifiers mocked, so no network is needed. They cover decoders, ingress limits, end-to-end scans of synthetic hidden-text images (QR, mirrored, faint), fusion and fail-safe policy rules, and the output guard's distinction between obeying an injected instruction and merely quoting it. Tour step 14 lists them as the extraction, fusion and policy suites.

sections.title: Imports and image helpers
sections.explanation: The repository root goes onto `sys.path`, and the tests import the real modules under test. `png` serialises a PIL image and `text_image` renders text in a chosen grey level, optionally mirrored. These synthetic images drive the OCR and orientation-recovery paths without any external fixtures.

sections.title: Mocked classifier fixtures
sections.explanation: `fake_llm` uses `monkeypatch` to replace `llm.classify_items` with a keyword-based stand-in and pins `prompt_guard_score` to a low value. Detection outcomes then depend only on what extraction recovers from the image, which is the behaviour under test. The `guard` fixture builds a `ThreatGuard` with audit logging off.
