sections.title: Decoder and ingress tests
sections.explanation: The base64 decoder must reassemble a payload split across lines while ignoring long plain words that happen to look like base64. The word-map test checks that substitution direction is inferred correctly. The ingress tests check that non-image bytes and over-long prompts are rejected, and that large images are downscaled to the configured model-view size.

sections.title: End-to-end hidden-text scans
sections.explanation: A benign recipe image must be allowed. A QR code carrying an override instruction must be blocked, with a `qr` segment in the evidence. Mirrored text must be recovered with method `un-mirror` and then blocked. Faint light-grey text must be recovered by a low-contrast or contrast-boost pass and must not be allowed. Each test asserts both the decision and *how* the text was found.

sections.title: Fusion and fail-safe policy
sections.explanation: The `_r` helper builds `DetectorResult` objects. These tests check key design rules: obfuscation alone can never reach REVIEW (it only amplifies other signals), overlapping harm and composite signals are not double-counted, and a failed required detector, an OCR failure, or a full classifier outage results in REVIEW with `fail_safe` set rather than ALLOW. Together they show the engine fails closed.

sections.title: Output guard compliance cases
sections.explanation: `check_reply` must reject a reply that echoes a canary token that appeared only in image text, and accept a neutral description. The parametrised `complied` table, partly taken from real model replies, separates true obedience (bare token, token after the answer) from quoting or refusing (the instruction shown in quotes or a blockquote, a reply describing the attempt). It also checks edge cases such as apostrophes not counting as quotes.

tests/test_virodh.py.overview: Pytest suite for the Virodh gateway. It runs end to end through FastAPI's TestClient with a fake guard engine, a fake upstream provider (httpx.MockTransport), a fake adversarial engine and a temporary SQLite store, so there are no network calls. It covers auth, decisions and actions per policy, operator rules, the OpenAI wire format, resilience (rate limits, fail-closed, load shedding, cache, circuit breaker), the scan API and the admin console. Tour step 14 covers it as the gateway end-to-end suite.

sections.title: Imports and helpers
sections.explanation: The tests import the real gateway app, `build_state`, config and security helpers. `ADMIN_TOKEN` is an obvious test placeholder, not a real secret. `png` and `data_url` build tiny inline images for multimodal messages.

sections.title: Fake guard, upstream, adversarial
sections.explanation: `FakeGuard` runs the *real* ingress validation (so malformed images still raise) but decides from keywords. The 'image text' for each image is registered by SHA-256, so tests control what extraction 'finds'. It also exposes switches for call counting, delays and injected exceptions. `FakeUpstream` records every forwarded request (URL, auth header, body) and can return error statuses. `FakeAdv` and `ADV_SUSPICIOUS` simulate the adversarial engine for chosen images.

sections.title: Environment fixture and request helpers
sections.explanation: The `env` fixture patches the adversarial hook, sets placeholder provider keys and a temporary DB path, tightens the concurrency and breaker settings, and installs a gateway state built on `httpx.MockTransport`. It cleans up the store and config afterwards. `make_key`, `chat` and `img_msg` keep each test focused on its assertions rather than request plumbing.

sections.title: Auth and core decisions
sections.explanation: These tests check the main security contract. Missing or invalid keys get 401 and nothing reaches the upstream. Benign requests are forwarded with a system message marking image content as untrusted, the inspected image bytes, and the *provider* key instead of the client's. Harmful or hidden-instruction requests are blocked and never forwarded. Strict policies return a 400 `content_filter` error. REVIEW is blocked unless the policy forwards it, and monitor mode forwards while recording what it would have blocked. The output guard withholds replies that obey hidden text, earlier conversation turns are inspected too, and adversarial flags are enforced only by strict policies.

sections.title: Operator rules
sections.explanation: `_policy_with` clones the default policy with overrides. Blocked phrases must match text recovered from the image (whitespace-normalised, whole words only). The denied-topic check is monkeypatched to show both a topic block and fail-safe behaviour: if the topic classifier raises, the result is REVIEW with `fail_safe` and the request is blocked, not allowed.

sections.title: Wire format and input validation
sections.explanation: Streaming requests are inspected as non-streaming calls upstream and then re-emitted as SSE chunks ending in `[DONE]`, with usage and `virodh` metadata included. Unsupported content, disabled remote images, invalid images, unknown models, bad JSON and oversized bodies are all rejected before forwarding. With remote images enabled, the SSRF test checks that loopback, link-local metadata, private ranges, embedded credentials and `file://` URLs are refused. The per-key model allow-list is enforced for both chat and `/v1/models`.

sections.title: Resilience behaviour
sections.explanation: The tests cover a per-key 429 with `Retry-After`, a guard exception failing closed with a 503 `inspection_unavailable`, load shedding with a 503 `overloaded` when the scan queue is full, identical inspections served from cache without a new guard call, upstream errors passed through with their status and `Retry-After`, and the circuit breaker opening after repeated 500s so the provider is no longer called.

sections.title: Scan API and admin console
sections.explanation: The scan endpoint returns evidence and `would_forward: false` and never calls the upstream. Admin access needs the console header plus a token. `_req` builds raw Starlette requests to test loopback rules, including rejecting a wrong `Host` header (a DNS-rebinding defence) and remote clients. Other tests check that the key list exposes only a prefix (never the hash or the full key), that revocation takes effect immediately, that invalid policies are rejected and the default policy cannot be deleted, and that the playground runs the same pipeline as the API.

deploy/Dockerfile.overview: CPU-only production image for the Virodh gateway, based on python:3.11-slim. It installs OpenCV/RapidOCR runtime libraries and CPU PyTorch, runs as an unprivileged user, keeps secrets out of the image, and adds a /readyz health check. Tour step 15 describes it as the container that docker-compose scales behind nginx.

sections.title: Base image and system libraries
sections.explanation: A slim Python 3.11 base keeps the image small. The environment variables turn off bytecode files, output buffering, the pip cache and pip's version check. `libgl1` and `libglib2.0-0` are the shared libraries OpenCV and RapidOCR need at runtime, and the apt lists are deleted in the same layer to save space.

sections.title: Dependency install
sections.explanation: `requirements.txt` is copied and installed *before* the rest of the source, so Docker can reuse the dependency layer when only code changes. Torch and torchvision come from the CPU wheel index first, which avoids pulling multi-gigabyte CUDA builds. This matches the project's CPU-only deployment target.

sections.title: Non-root user and runtime env
sections.explanation: A system user with a fixed UID (10001) owns only the writable paths: the `/data` volume for the SQLite DB, logs and cache. The container runs as this user. API keys and the admin token are passed in at runtime and never baked into the image. The safe defaults turn off prompt previews in logs and turn off tokenless loopback admin access, which would be unsafe inside container networking. Port 8000 is exposed.

sections.title: Health check and start command
sections.explanation: The `HEALTHCHECK` uses Python's standard library to hit `/readyz`, so no curl is needed in the image. A 60-second start period allows for model and OCR warm-up. The command starts one worker per container behind a proxy and trusts forwarded headers, because scaling is meant to happen through replicas (`docker compose --scale`). The comment notes that several workers per container also work on Linux.

deploy/docker-compose.yml.overview: Docker Compose definition for the production-style Virodh AI cluster. It builds one image from deploy/Dockerfile, runs it as a horizontally scalable `virodh` service, and puts an nginx container in front as the single public entry point on port 8080. This is the production half of tour step 15 (Deployment and Scaling), and it works together with deploy/nginx/virodh.conf, which it mounts into the nginx container.

sections.title: Usage header and project name
sections.explanation: The comment block is the operator runbook. It lists which API keys and the admin token to supply through the environment or a `.env` file that stays uncommitted, shows the `--scale virodh=3` command, and lists the public URLs. It also points out an easy-to-miss step: nginx resolves replica addresses when it loads its config, so it has to be reloaded after the replica count changes. `name: virodh` fixes the Compose project name, so container and volume names don't depend on the directory name.

sections.title: Gateway service build and secrets
sections.explanation: The `virodh` service builds from the repository root (`context: ..`), so the Dockerfile can copy the whole project. The model-provider keys use `${VAR:-}`, which falls back to an empty value, so any provider can be missing. `VIRODH_ADMIN_TOKEN` uses `${VAR:?message}`, which makes Compose refuse to start when it is unset. The cluster therefore can't come up with an unprotected admin console.

sections.title: Runtime tuning environment
sections.explanation: All replicas on one host share a single SQLite database on the shared volume; the comment says it relies on WAL mode for concurrent access. Prompt previews are turned off, so logs hold only hashes. Loopback trust is also turned off, because every request arrives from the nginx proxy and a loopback address no longer means a trusted local caller. Scan concurrency, OCR threads and `OMP_NUM_THREADS` are capped low, so several CPU-only replicas can share the host's cores without oversubscribing them.

sections.title: Volumes, limits and hardening
sections.explanation: Two named volumes keep state when containers are recreated: `virodh-data` holds the database, and `model-cache` keeps the downloaded ResNet18 weights so each new replica doesn't fetch them again. `expose` opens port 8000 only on the internal Compose network, so no host port is published and traffic must pass through nginx. Each replica is limited to 2 GB of memory, and `no-new-privileges` stops processes from gaining privileges through setuid binaries.

sections.title: nginx front proxy and volumes
sections.explanation: The nginx service uses the official alpine image and publishes only host port 8080. It mounts virodh.conf read-only as the default site, replacing the stock config. `depends_on` controls only start order and does not wait for the gateway to be healthy; nginx's `max_fails` settings in virodh.conf cover a replica that isn't ready yet. The named volumes are declared at the bottom with default settings.

deploy/nginx/virodh.conf.overview: nginx site configuration for the reverse proxy and load balancer in front of the Virodh gateway replicas. It defines the upstream pool, a coarse per-IP rate limit, proxy timeouts sized for slow inspections, and per-path routing. Admin and metrics endpoints are open only to private networks. It is mounted by deploy/docker-compose.yml and supports the scaling story in tour step 15.

sections.title: Upstream pool
sections.explanation: `least_conn` sends each request to the replica with the fewest open connections. The comment explains why: an inspection can take seconds, so round-robin could pile requests onto one busy replica. The single `server virodh:8000` entry relies on Docker DNS, which returns every replica of the scaled service when nginx loads its config. `max_fails`/`fail_timeout` take a failing replica out of rotation for a short time, and `keepalive 64` keeps upstream connections open for reuse. The header comment notes that TLS still has to be added for a real deployment.

sections.title: Per-IP rate limit zone
sections.explanation: This sets up a 10 MB shared-memory zone keyed by the binary client IP, with a limit of 20 requests per second. The comment calls it a coarse protection against request floods only. The finer per-API-key limits are handled inside the Virodh application, so nginx doesn't need to know about keys.

sections.title: Server-wide proxy settings
sections.explanation: `server_tokens off` hides the nginx version. `client_max_body_size 12m` is kept in sync with the application's `server.max_body_mb` setting, so the proxy and the app reject oversized uploads at the same size. HTTP/1.1 with an empty `Connection` header is needed for upstream keepalive, and the `X-Forwarded-*` headers pass the real client IP and scheme to the gateway. The 180 s read timeout leaves room for an inspection plus a model call. `proxy_next_upstream error timeout` retries on another replica only when the first one couldn't be reached or timed out.

sections.title: Gateway API location
sections.explanation: The per-IP limit is applied to `/v1/`, the client-facing API. `burst=40 nodelay` lets short spikes through right away, and requests over the limit get HTTP 429 instead of nginx's default 503. `proxy_buffering off` is needed so server-sent-event streaming responses reach the client as they are produced and aren't held back in nginx's buffer.

sections.title: Restricted admin and metrics
sections.explanation: `/admin/` and the exact path `/metrics` are allowed only from loopback and the RFC 1918 private ranges; all other clients are denied. This network check is a second layer on top of the admin token, which the comment says is still required. The exact-match `location =` keeps the rule on `/metrics` from applying to other paths that begin with that prefix.

sections.title: Catch-all location
sections.explanation: Every other path goes to the backend without rate limiting or IP restrictions: the website, docs, console UI and health probes. Because nginx picks the most specific prefix, the `/v1/` and `/admin/` rules above take priority over this catch-all.

start_virodh.ps1.overview: PowerShell launcher for running Virodh AI locally on Windows. It builds the React web app and installs the Node server's dependencies if needed, starts the Python inspection engine on port 8000, waits for its readiness probe, then starts the Node dashboard backend on port 3000. It is the local-development half of tour step 15, as opposed to the Docker/nginx production setup.

sections.title: Usage notes and strict mode
sections.explanation: The header shows how to run the script with `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` and notes that the first account to sign up becomes the admin. `$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"` makes PowerShell errors stop the script instead of letting it continue. `$PSScriptRoot` anchors every path to the script's own directory, so it works from any current directory.

sections.title: One-time build steps
sections.explanation: The checks run steps only when needed. The React app is built with `npm install` plus `npx vite build` only if `web/dist/index.html` is missing, and the server's dependencies are installed only if `server/node_modules` is missing. As a result, later runs are fast, but the script won't rebuild the frontend after source changes until `web/dist` is deleted. `Push-Location`/`Pop-Location` change into each folder temporarily, and a `logs` directory is created ahead of time.

sections.title: Start engine and wait for readiness
sections.explanation: The Python engine is started from the project's `.venv` interpreter through `scripts/virodh_serve.py` with 2 workers on port 8000, in a minimized window. `-PassThru` returns the process so its PID can be shown later. The script then polls `/readyz` every 2 seconds, up to 90 times (about 3 minutes), and swallows connection errors while the engine is still starting. If the engine never becomes ready, the loop just ends and the dashboard starts anyway, so the script does not fail hard.

sections.title: Start dashboard and report PIDs
sections.explanation: The Node dashboard backend (`server/src/index.js`) is started with Node's experimental-feature warning turned off. It serves the built React app on port 3000. At the end, the script prints both URLs and a ready-to-paste `Stop-Process` command with both PIDs, because both processes keep running after the script exits.

eval/adversarial/write_summary.py.overview: Builds the dashboard adversarial summary report from the loop and generalization result files, without any hand-typed numbers.

eval/baseline_summary.py.overview: Summarises unguarded model responses: coverage, keyword-heuristic refusal rate and canary-hijack rate, using the output guard compliance check.
